Solomon’s mind was on the people. He did not ask for four hundred women or chariots, or to be a king of 4,000; he asked for “an understanding heart to judge thy people”, “for who is able to judge this thy so great a people?” Because he had a mind for the people, the Lord elevated him and gave him more than he even desired for himself. Likewise with us: when we have a mind for the people, the Lord will bless that thing beyond measure.

Sirach says it plainly: “Consider that I laboured not for myself only, but for all them that seek learning.” In this truth we are not doing this for ourselves. Captains left at four in the morning, driving, so they could be here to help teach the class. A captain drove down and got here at five in the morning to check the congregation, to check on the saints of the Most High. The bishops travel all over the world; the deacons travel. This is not for ourselves; this is for the nation of Israel, because we understand the kingdom that is at hand.

“but for all them”: this is a nation. You must be nation-minded. A lot of times we are not like that: me, me, me, me, me, and that is all you are concerned with. But all through the Bible the greatest leaders were focused on the nation of Israel and how to move the nation further ahead.

That is the mindset of a leader and the action of a king: like Solomon, labour not for yourself only, but for all the people, and the Lord gives more than you asked.

“Notwithstanding the Lord stood with me, and strengthened me; that by me the preaching might be fully known”. The Lord stood with Paul and strengthened him, so that the preaching might go forth by him.

That is our job: we must strengthen one another. You get weak at different times. You need counsel. You need some exhortation. You have to vent sometimes. And it is your job as a leader to be there to strengthen each other, as the Lord stood with Paul.

So those who have the rule over you and speak the word of God unto you are there to strengthen you, and when you are strengthened, you follow their faith and do the same for those around you.

“And after he had spent some time there, he departed, and went over all the country of Galatia and Phrygia in order, strengthening all the disciples.” Paul went country to country strengthening all the disciples. That is the job of a leader, and it shows how a leader transfers his belief onto others.

The same work goes on today. As the bishops and the deacons trailblazed the way, the captains follow the same path, and when they go to these places they continue to build our people up worldwide. A captain just back from Guyana reports that the brothers and sisters there in South America are growing tremendously, doing real good. The Lord has good things for them.

Like Paul in Galatia and Phrygia, the leaders go out to the nations where our people are and strengthen the disciples there.

Moses prayed, “I pray thee, let me go over, and see the good land that is beyond Jordan, that goodly mountain, and Lebanon. But the Lord was wroth with me for your sakes, and would not hear me”. He was told, “Let it suffice thee; speak no more unto me of this matter”, and to go up to the top of Pisgah and behold the land with his eyes, “for thou shalt not go over this Jordan.”

Moses could not cross over, but look at what he was charged to do: “But charge Joshua, and encourage him, and strengthen him: for he shall go over before this people, and he shall cause them to inherit the land which thou shalt see.” Charge him, encourage him, strengthen him.

That is your job as a leader: to encourage and strengthen the men around you. A leader transfers his belief onto the next man, so that the one coming after him can lead the people into what he himself was given to see. That is part of the faith that those who have the rule over you pass on.

“Behold, thou hast instructed many, and thou hast strengthened the weak hands.” Your job as a leader is to instruct many. And your job is to strengthen the weak hands.

It is your job to build the brothers and the sisters up in the spirit. That is part of how a leader transfers his belief onto others: those who have the rule over you and have spoken unto you the word of God instruct you, and when your hands are weak they strengthen them, so that you can follow their faith.

Christ told Peter, “But I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not: and when thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren.” When you convert, strengthen your brothers. That is the charge that goes with the faith that is passed on to you.

Read on and Peter answers, “Lord, I am ready to go with thee, both into prison, and to death”, and Christ answers that before the cock crows Peter will thrice deny that he knows him. Christ prayed that Peter's faith would not fail, knowing what was coming, and still gave him the work of strengthening his brethren.

This is the leader transferring his belief onto others. Christ imparted his faith to Peter, and Peter was to impart it to the brethren. The one who has been strengthened turns around and strengthens the next man.

Christ answered Peter, “Blessed art thou, Simon Bar–jona: for flesh and blood hath not revealed it unto thee, but my Father which is in heaven.” Then he told him, “thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.”

How do you think that made Peter feel? Christ telling you, I am going to build my church upon you. That is what great leaders do. Good leaders make you believe in them; great leaders make you believe in you. They empower others, they strengthen others, they make you believe in yourself and not in them.

That is how a leader transfers his belief onto others, the faith Hebrews 13:7 tells us to follow. It is how the Bishop is able to raise up other bishops, raise up deacons, raise up captains, and soldiers by the thousands. Great leaders raise up more leaders.

This is the rebuilding of Jerusalem. “Next unto him repaired Uzziel the son of Harhaiah, of the goldsmiths. Next unto him also repaired Hananiah the son of one of the apothecaries, and they fortified Jerusalem unto the broad wall.” Each man repaired his own section of the wall. Then: “And next unto them repaired Rephaiah the son of Hur, the ruler of the half part of Jerusalem.” The ruler of the half part: he was a supervisor over that area.

That is leadership. When you come in the truth you may just edit the video, go on the fly mission, or work in the kitchen. At some point you become over the office: now you are over the brothers that are editing, over the IT team, over the building team, over the sisters. Now your job changes, because you have people under you. Everybody is not built for that level. You are not in charge; you are responsible for those in your charge. In IUIC there are different offices with leads in place, and a man who was once responsible for one office, the Lord entrusted him with more.

Sometimes brothers get overwhelmed, and that will happen. But there is no better thing than to be overwhelmed for the Lord. You do not have a demon on your back, you are not behind bars, you are not suffering illness; you are stressed out for the Lord's work, and that is a beautiful thing. So do not complain. Come up and say, I need more assistance in this office. Pray and fast for more laborers, and rejoice in it, because the Lord gave you that office and put you in that position.

Job 33:23 speaks of “a messenger with him, an interpreter, one among a thousand”. You are the interpreter, brother, and you are that one among a thousand. When you are one among a thousand, that makes you a leader, and you have to have the mind of a leader. Any place you step into, your mindset shouldn't be to fit in; you should be figuring out how to make it better. Joseph didn't go into Egypt and just sit there; he asked how we are going to solve the problem. The Lord gave us wisdom, discretion, judgment and skill sets.

The first thing in the mindset of a leader is that he believes he can get the job done. That is what separates you from everybody else. When an issue arises, you don't run. You raise your hand, you volunteer, you figure out a solution to the problem.

Isaiah shows it: “Also I heard the voice of the Lord, saying, Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” Who is going to go on our behalf? “Then said I, Here am I; send me.” That's the mindset of a leader.

That is the same thing David did. Everybody kept crying about the situation, and David said, where is Goliath at? Show me. The first thing you have to have is a willingness and a belief in completing the task, whatever it may be, and that mindset alone sets you apart. That is what the Lord has put in your spirit to do: not an unsure mind that says maybe I can, but send me.

“For I know not to give flattering titles; in so doing my maker would soon take me away.” When you get the flattering title, your maker soon takes you away. What does that mean? You want the flattering title, you get the test, you fail the test. Bam. Thought I was worthy. Nope.

So be mindful of what you ask for. Brothers work underhandedly to become leaders, and it don't work like that; this is the Lord's business, and he is the one giving it out. Brothers that ask for rank, that say give me the 50's test, never make it, and that is how you know Satan is pushing them. When brothers ask for the test, nine times out of ten they fail it, because spiritually you are not ready if you are asking. Nobody asks to be a leader. The Lord raised all these men up. The Bishop didn't ask to be a bishop; he became a bishop. If you are asking for it, you are in the wrong place.

When the student is ready, the teacher will be there. The Lord will place you where you are supposed to be; promotion comes from the Lord, and there is a reason you are in the position you are in. Once you fulfill that office, the Lord will make it happen. Many brothers who wanted position fell down and never made it back, while others who were down came back on fire. The work determines where you are supposed to be. Brothers get jealous when another brother gets position, but if you love the Lord you work for the Lord, not for position. In Maccabees the brother who said let me get me a name ended up put to death.

That is what Judith 8:24 asks of a leader: not a title, but “let us shew an example to our brethren, because their hearts depend upon us”. The higher up you go, the more people you serve. If you don't have the mindset to build up those beneath you and to support and push up the leader above you, forget it; the Lord can't use you.

Christ walked by the sea of Galilee and said to Peter and Andrew, “Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men.” Baruch shows where that invitation comes from.

“He hath found out all the way of knowledge, and hath given it unto Jacob his servant, and to Israel his beloved.” All the understanding and wisdom was given to us, not to the other nations. So there is no reason for you to sit on that wisdom and do nothing.

“Afterward did he shew himself upon earth, and conversed with men.” That is speaking of Christ. We are the only ones that have a God; the other nations do not. Our God saw us as so special that he showed himself on the earth. Our God, Emmanuel, walked with us and conversed with us. That goes back to Matthew 4 when he said “Follow me”: that was our leader telling us to follow him.

So we are not supposed to just sit here and do absolutely nothing. Our God saw fit to walk with us, teach us and guide us, and we have to do the same thing: teach our brothers and sisters and wake them up. The invitation is there, and like Peter and Andrew, who “straightway left their nets, and followed him”, we have to accept it.

This is our job. “And now, saith the Lord that formed me from the womb to be his servant, to bring Jacob again to him”. You were made to be the servant of God. You were made to do this work. You were not born to be a basketball player or a rapper. You were born to be a servant of God; that is our duty and our calling. “To bring Jacob again to him”: that is your commission.

“Though Israel be not gathered, yet shall I be glorious in the eyes of the Lord, and my God shall be my strength.”

“And he said, It is a light thing that thou shouldest be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel”. Think about that: it is a light thing. It is the least you can do. The Lord sacrificed himself for you; our God came down and walked with us. It is a light thing to do the work of the Lord and go wake up your people.

“I will also give thee for a light to the Gentiles, that thou mayest be my salvation unto the end of the earth.” That is the same thing read in Matthew 4: Galilee of the Gentiles, the people that sat in darkness, saw great light. It is talking about Israel; we are to go to our brothers of the Northern Kingdom and be the light to the Gentiles, carrying on the mission God gave us.

“So built we the wall”: all through our history, the forefathers were building. What we are doing today is nothing different from what they always did, and Ezekiel shows the kind of building the Lord gives us while we are scattered.

“Although I have cast them far off among the heathen, and although I have scattered them among the countries, yet will I be to them as a little sanctuary in the countries where they shall come.” Israel was cast far off and scattered, and the Lord still gave them little sanctuaries in the lands where they came.

When Paul went to Galatia, to Colossae, to Corinth and to Thessalonica, those were sanctuaries, just like the ones you see today. The schools are those little sanctuaries in the countries, and each and every one of us put a hand into building each and every one of them.

So the wall of Nehemiah and the little sanctuary of Ezekiel are the same work. The people built because they had a mind to work, and that mind to work is what leadership has to put into the people now.

The people built the wall because they “had a mind to work.” This is how a leader’s mindset must be, and Christ shows it: “The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light.”

A single eye is being locked in, what they call laser focus. Whatever you are locked in on, that is what you are going to see. That is all you are going to see, and that is all that matters.

And when the leader is like that, guess who else is going to be like that? Everybody underneath him. The single eye of the one at the head fills the whole body with light, so the whole camp takes on his focus.

That is why the wall got built. The mind to work in the people starts with the mind of the one leading them.

“A wise judge will instruct his people; and the government of a prudent man is well ordered. As the judge of the people is himself, so are his officers; and what manner of man the ruler of the city is, such are all they that dwell therein.” However the leader is, that is how the men under him are going to be.

So when you see these other camps that look disorganized, that are talking about rape, that have not built anything in years, find their leaders, and that is what you will see. When you see us traveling all over the world, building institutions, organizations within the organization, look at our leaders. We are the representation of our leadership.

When we go to Chicago we are not on film eating chicken and pizza in the hood at midnight. How is that a leader of a congregation? You will never see a bishop or a deacon put out a video like that. When we went to Chicago, we went to O’Block teaching the word of the Lord.

Everything rises and falls on leadership. There are cities where the leader was changed and the camp took off, and other places where the leader left and everything fell apart. You are who your leader is. That is why everybody wants to ask the Bishop for the secret sauce, but what they do not understand is that Christ is at the head and we are all following Christ. The Most High is building 144,000 leaders, sealed with the law of God, and nothing they try can stop it.

That is why the people of Nehemiah had a mind to work: the wall reflects the ones leading the building.
blog/2026/2026-03-21-2026-03-21-much-is-:
“For thou art an holy people unto the Lord thy God: the Lord thy God hath chosen thee to be a special people unto himself”. He chose you to be special unto him, set apart from everybody else. So the question is: what makes us holy? What scripture?

Leviticus 20:26 was brought from the floor as the answer: “And ye shall be holy unto me: for I the Lord am holy, and have severed you from other people, that ye should be mine.” The Lord is holy, and he severed Israel from other people to be his. That severing is the same set-apart people of Deuteronomy 7:6, chosen “above all people that are upon the face of the earth.”

So there has to be something we are doing that makes us different. We cannot be doing the same thing the world is doing, and we cannot be doing what the churches are doing. What severs us from the other people is the laws of God being applied, which is what Romans 7:12 goes on to show.

“But when he saw the multitudes, he was moved with compassion on them, because they fainted, and were scattered abroad, as sheep having no shepherd.” As Christ went out teaching, healing and doing miracles, he looked and saw that his people fainted. They were out in the streets, they did not worship their God, and their own leaders were taking advantage of them at that time.

It is the same in this captivity as in the time of Rome. Look at our people out there: they are lost, they have no shepherd, they are confused. Not only have the people of the world taken advantage of us, but our own people take advantage too, using the knowledge to get preeminence.

So leaders are motivated because we see the same thing Christ saw: our people afflicted, with no leaders, and looking for a shepherd, which is Christ ultimately. Instead of benefiting ourselves, we see the decayed state of our people and make the sacrifices. To hell with the riches, to hell with the women, having sex, and all those other things. We do whatever it takes to rebuild our nation, so that we can truly benefit from each other and have one shepherd rule over us, with nobody able to take advantage of us.

That is the mind the Lord has put in us, and those who carry it are the ones standing in these last days, speaking with authority and showing our people: this is not the way; let us move according to this holy word and restore this nation. That is what it means to be the holy people God chose.

“Wherefore the law is holy, and the commandment holy, and just, and good.” If the law is holy, and God says you are a holy people, then we are supposed to be a law-abiding people. The laws of God are our constitution, the thing we stand on. That is what makes us holy, what makes us special, what makes us set apart: the laws being applied.

The word of God has no power unless you activate it, and the only way to activate it is to do what it says to do. Other than that it is just pages, just words on a page, just a book. The word is alive and living when you let it live through you by your actions. You become the word, the living example of what it means to be a holy people. That is why the nations say, what a wise and understanding people. They see our actions.

We witness that already at the big events in the big arenas. They say, thousands of black men and nobody smoking weed, no fights breaking out. Then look at what happened in Houston at the rodeo, and how they laughed at us; we are a joke to them. But when we move they ask, how are they so organized, how can they mobilize a few thousand men, put them on the street and file them back in like that, nobody fighting and the place clean? That is the word of God working through us. There is a standard we live by because we are gods on the earth, and it is second nature to us as a nation.

So do not walk in hypocrisy. God gave us something that will make us shine bright and obtain the kingdom. Be that living example to the people.

“There is one that is wise and teacheth many, and yet is unprofitable to himself.” You cannot be a hypocrite, especially in a leadership position. Look at the other camps: they are supposed to be leading the people, but their mind is on the riches, or on how many bodies they can put as a notch in their belt.

There is one that is supposed to be wise. What makes you wise? Keeping the commandments. Those leaders know that. They know they are Israel, they know they are God's chosen people, and they know they are supposed to be keeping the laws. Yet because of their bad intentions and covetousness, because their god is money, or their god is power to move and persuade the people, they are unprofitable to themselves.

And nothing will be hid. Everything that is done will be revealed in time. That is the other side of Deuteronomy 7: the Lord “keepeth covenant and mercy with them that love him and keep his commandments to a thousand generations; And repayeth them that hate him to their face, to destroy them”. If you use a position to lead and teach the people and then take advantage of them, beguiling the sisters into sex, keeping them in a filthy mindset, or taking their money, God will judge you. You hate God and you hate his people.

God said, “Let us make man in our image, after our likeness”. God's image is the greatest image there is, and he mirrored man after himself, then gave him dominion and rulership. “And God blessed them”. But the blessing did not end with his image and dominion. In chapter 2, “the Lord God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.”

The breath of life is wisdom, and it is what activated us. The word of God has to activate your life. God gave us laws to govern us so that we could be that special people; without them we would be just like every other nation. We are at the lowest state right now because we sinned against God, but we do not want to share power with any nation or be all-inclusive. God wants all or none, and we wait in this state until he puts us back in our rightful place.

Wisdom of Solomon 7 shows what that breath is. Wisdom, “which is the worker of all things, taught me: for in her is an understanding spirit”. That is why we understand the Bible and have a scripture for everything we say. She is “Kind to man, steadfast, sure, free from care, having all power, overseeing all things”. Free from care means free from the cares of this world. Mark 4 names them: “the cares of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches, and the lusts of other things entering in, choke the word, and it becometh unfruitful.” Wisdom says beware of covetousness, so you do not entertain it.

Then the verse that ties it to Genesis 2: “For she is the breath of the power of God, and a pure influence flowing from the glory of the Almighty: therefore can no defiled thing fall into her.” Wisdom flows down from the Almighty and molds you, so if she is influencing you, you are tethered to God. Otherwise something else, covetousness or lust, is influencing you. That breath is what God gave us in Genesis 2, and we let something else draw us away. God gave us everything, and we were led away by women, money, riches and cars, as if the things he created were greater than him.

The power of God is his word. Hebrews 4 says “the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword”, the same words used of wisdom, and it “is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.” Psalms 19 names the pure influence: “The law of the Lord is perfect, converting the soul: the testimony of the Lord is sure, making wise the simple.” “the commandment of the Lord is pure, enlightening the eyes.” We were once simple; now wisdom makes us wise and we see clearly. In 1 Samuel 10:6 the Spirit of the Lord comes and a man is “turned into another man.”

Much is given, so much is required. Christ asks, “why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?” The one who hears and does is like the man who “laid the foundation on a rock”, and that foundation lets you endure tribulation; the one who hears and does not is the house that falls. Learn yourself before chasing deep prophecy: get off the sin first. Wisdom is “the unspotted mirror of the power of God”, and James says pure religion is “to keep himself unspotted from the world.” “remaining in herself, she maketh all things new”. Tether yourself to wisdom and she makes you new.

People are watching. A sister came to the truth because she saw the camp in the streets and not one brother tried to talk to her. That is the right example: a people made in God's image, living by the breath he gave, set apart from every other nation.

Isaiah 61 says to “proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord”, and Isaiah 49 says it again: “Thus saith the Lord, In an acceptable time have I heard thee, and in a day of salvation have I helped thee: and I will preserve thee, and give thee for a covenant of the people, to establish the earth, to cause to inherit the desolate heritages.” The acceptable year and the acceptable time: that is when we heal the broken heart and proclaim liberty to the captives.

“The Lord hath called me from the womb; from the bowels of my mother hath he made mention of my name. And he hath made my mouth like a sharp sword; in the shadow of his hand hath he hid me, and made me a polished shaft; in his quiver hath he hid me; And said unto me, Thou art my servant, O Israel, in whom I will be glorified.” We are supposed to glorify our God in this body.

“Then I said, I have laboured in vain, I have spent my strength for nought, and in vain: yet surely my judgment is with the Lord, and my work with my God.” We go to stiff-necked, hard-hearted people who refuse to hear the word of God, but we still proclaim the day of the Lord to heal those minds and tell them there is an end to this: we will rule one day. He formed us from the womb “to bring Jacob again to him.”

“It is a light thing that thou shouldest be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel.” It may not appear that we are doing it, but when the numbers come in, it is a light thing he has given us, and he still charges us to raise up the children of Israel. “I will also give thee for a light to the Gentiles, that thou mayest be my salvation unto the end of the earth”: that goes back to Matthew 4, the Gentiles of Galilee. Our job is to bring salvation to the people and lead them back to him, and that is a great ministry.

“Kings shall see and arise, princes also shall worship” … “and he shall choose thee.” Out of all of them, he is going to choose us. And unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required: we want to be the faithful servant the Lord finds doing this work in sincerity, without deceit and without secret sins.

“The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me; because the Lord hath anointed me to preach good tidings unto the meek; he hath sent me to bind up the brokenhearted.” He has chosen and set apart every man here, all the captains, to preach good tidings to the meek. But how do you bind up a person that is broken? The brokenhearted are broken in the mind: suffering the curses without knowing the will of God. We are set apart to bind them up. What do we bind them with?

“Bind up the testimony, seal the law among my disciples.” We bind up the testimony and seal the law in the minds of the people, because they are brokenhearted and their minds are broken. That is what we are called to do: to bind them to the laws of God.

And we show them why it is good. Look at our lives as the example of what it means to serve God and why it is good to serve him. That means we have to be sincere about it. How do we tell the people to touch not the unclean thing and then not live it ourselves? The one who was profitable to many but not to himself will be punished accordingly, because he knew better.

So the good tidings we proclaim with the law are these: if we repent and keep God's laws in sincerity and endure to the end, he will deliver us, and we will rule again, as we were made in his image to rule.

Christ says “that servant, which knew his lord’s will, and prepared not himself, neither did according to his will, shall be beaten with many stripes.” What is the will of God? David defines it: “I delight to do thy will, O my God: yea, thy law is within my heart.”

God defines his will as his law. His will for us is that we keep the commandments. So the servant in Luke 12:47 who knew his Lord's will is the one who knew the laws of God and prepared not himself.

Preparing yourself means measuring yourself against the Bible, men and women alike. The Bible is the measuring barometer we look at to see whether we are pairing ourselves off right with God. If we are really honest and examine ourselves, in many cases we are not: if Christ came back right now, many of us are not ready. It comes down to opening the book, reading it for what it says, and doing what it says.

Much was given to us. We have the keys to the kingdom of heaven: the will of God, which people live a whole life and never understand, thinking a Hail Mary or gospel songs will have them holding hands with Jesus in the kingdom, not knowing that believing is an action word. Because we know his will, much more will be required of us, and as you move up in rank the road gets narrower until you have to walk blameless. We tell the people to do this and not do that, so we had better live it, or we will be beaten with many stripes.

Wisdom says, “Riches and honour are with me; yea, durable riches and righteousness. My fruit is better than gold, yea, than fine gold.” What are those riches? Colossians shows it: “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.”

The riches we are looking for are not money, though people think they are. We need the durable riches, which is wisdom: the word of Christ dwelling in us richly. And this is what we are supposed to do with it: teach and admonish one another.

God says, I am giving it to you. But you are walking in hypocrisy, distracted by covetousness, and a man’s life does not consist of the abundance of what he has. That was not their kingdom at that point, and all of this is coming to an end anyway. God has something far better than what you are looking at, and you are about to throw it away for this world.

Now you understand what the scripture is saying, so you have no excuse. Much is given, so much is required, and the one who knew will be beaten with many stripes. So I have to walk in that, stand in that space and be that, or get ready to get beat. The durable riches of Proverbs 8 are the word living in us richly, and they have to be walked in.

Sirach says of David, “In all his works he praised the Holy One most high with words of glory; with his whole heart he sung songs, and loved him that made him.” But didn't David sin against God? He did. Yet “The Lord took away his sins, and exalted his horn for ever: he gave him a covenant of kings, and a throne of glory in Israel.” David sinned, but David repented, and God took away his sins.

This is how he repented: “For I acknowledge my transgressions: and my sin is ever before me. Against thee, thee only, have I sinned, and done this evil in thy sight: that thou mightest be justified when thou speakest, and be clear when thou judgest.” He confessed.

“Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean: wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow.” And after he confessed, what did David do? “Then will I teach transgressors thy ways; and sinners shall be converted unto thee.” Get myself right, and then I'm going to go teach the people.

He teaches them “That all the children of Israel might see that it is good to follow the Lord.” Look at my example: it is good to follow the Lord, because in the end the Lord chose me as his friend.

David is a famous man, and he is an example for all of us. Some of us err in this truth, but you can recover yourself and still earn a name. You just have to do the work and be sincere. Much is given and much is required of us as leaders, so we have to be honest, confess, get clean, and then lead the people back to God.

Psalms 19 showed the law converting the soul, and once converted we are new. 1 Samuel 10:6 says the same thing: “And the Spirit of the Lord will come upon thee, and thou shalt prophesy with them, and shalt be turned into another man.”

With the word of God you change into another man. That is what Wisdom of Solomon 7:27 means: “she maketh all things new.” Wisdom will make you new, so you can’t keep doing the same thing.

But if the word is dealing with you and you are still trying to live that old man, still letting that old man tell you what to do, still doing that same stuff, the Lord says, I am going to beat you with many stripes, because I gave you something and you weren’t listening. Much is given, much is required. And don’t think many stripes is a pow pow and that is it. Many in that day will say “Lord, Lord”, and he is going to say, I don’t know you.

Wisdom of Solomon 7:25 says wisdom is “the breath of the power of God.” What is the power of God? Hebrews 4 answers.

“For he that is entered into his rest, he also hath ceased from his own works, as God did from his. Let us labour therefore to enter into that rest, lest any man fall after the same example of unbelief.” We fought that example of unbelief. If we believe, we are tethered with God and following wisdom. Wisdom is pure, steadfast and sure, and we enter into that rest.

“For the word of God is quick, and powerful.” Wisdom of Solomon 7:22 just said wisdom is “quick”, and “having all power.” The same words. And it is “sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.”

The intents of the heart are where sin begins. So we want that pure influence, so that the intents of this mind are not led astray and what guides and directs us is the word of God. There should be something in all of us that says, I can’t do that, it is wrong to do that. If we turn aside from that, we are saying we are hypocrites and don’t really believe. God has chosen us, for whatever reason, to give us wisdom. The power of God is the word of God. It is wisdom.

Wisdom of Solomon 7:26: “For she is the brightness of the everlasting light, the unspotted mirror of the power of God, and the image of his goodness.” Wisdom is unspotted. James 1:27 shows how a man keeps himself the same way.

“Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.”

You keep yourself unspotted from the world by visiting the fatherless and the afflicted, all people afflicted in the mind. But you are too busy trying to bag the chick. She came out of the world, out of whatever she was doing, and instead of leading her to God you are trying to sleep with her.

If we want to know how to keep ourselves unspotted, we tether ourselves to God, because flowing down from him is wisdom. You come into this truth not knowing any better, wisdom flows down from God to you, you apply it, and you become new: “she maketh all things new.”

“A good man out of the good treasure of his heart bringeth forth that which is good; and an evil man out of the evil treasure of his heart bringeth forth that which is evil: for of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaketh.” What comes out of his mouth is what is in him.

“And why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?” Why are you calling me Lord, Lord, and don’t do the things I tell you to do? “Whosoever cometh to me, and heareth my sayings, and doeth them, I will shew you to whom he is like: He is like a man which built an house, and digged deep, and laid the foundation on a rock: and when the flood arose, the stream beat vehemently upon that house, and could not shake it: for it was founded upon a rock.” “But he that heareth, and doeth not, is like a man that without a foundation built an house upon the earth; against which the stream did beat vehemently, and immediately it fell.”

The one built on Christ, which is the rock, is the one that is applying it. Applying it is the whole key. That is what strengthens the foundation and lets us endure when tribulations come. Wisdom teaches us that, and it is plain to understand. In that day men will say, Lord, Lord, did not I prophesy? Yes, but you still didn’t do what I told you to do. You were out on the street teaching, but you were a hypocrite; you weren’t living it.

Brothers sometimes come up wanting to understand the deep prophecies. Brother, let’s first help you get off of Pornhub. Why are you in Revelation trying to understand these archangels? You have to let that stuff go. You know prophecy, but you don’t know you yet. Learn you, so you are able to live it, and then instruct people wisely and teach them how to serve God.

Wisdom of Solomon 7:23 says wisdom is “Kind to man, steadfast, sure, free from care.” Free from what care? Free from worry and stress, and above all free from the cares of this world. Mark 4 names them.

“And these are they which are sown among thorns; such as hear the word, And the cares of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches, and the lusts of other things entering in, choke the word, and it becometh unfruitful.” The cares of the world, the riches and the lusts of other things deceive you. Life does not consist in the abundance of things; they deceive you and choke the word.

Wisdom is free of those cares. The man that has wisdom is not going to be subject to the riches of this world. God said beware of covetousness, and that is wisdom, so I am going to beware of it; I am not going to entertain that.

So it is in our best interest to be paired with wisdom, because wisdom has “all power, overseeing all things.” Tether yourself to wisdom and you can see clearly, the cares of this world cannot choke the word, and it will not become unfruitful in you.

Wisdom is “a pure influence flowing from the glory of the Almighty: therefore can no defiled thing fall into her.” Influence means to mold you and direct you. If wisdom is flowing down from the Almighty and it is influencing you, you are connected, tethered, with God. Or something else can be influencing you, and that will not be wisdom; it will be covetousness, lust, whatever it might be. Psalms 19 shows what that pure influence is.

“The law of the Lord is perfect, converting the soul: the testimony of the Lord is sure, making wise the simple.” We were once simple, but wisdom is now in us, making us wise. “The statutes of the Lord are right, rejoicing the heart: the commandment of the Lord is pure, enlightening the eyes.”

That pure influence is the statutes, the laws of God. The commandment is “pure”, and it enlightens the eyes so that we can see clearly.

And if our eyes are enlightened and the Lord has converted us, what are we now? We are new, something different. That is where Wisdom of Solomon 7:27 goes: “remaining in herself, she maketh all things new.”

Wisdom of Solomon 7:27 says wisdom, “in all ages entering into holy souls, she maketh them friends of God, and prophets.” Wisdom cannot dwell in a body that is subject to sin, hypocrisy, covetousness or hatred. Ecclesiasticus 4:10 shows the conversion of our minds in these last days: when we put our interests over the Lord’s, it distances us from him, and when we put the Lord’s interests over ours, it brings us closer to the heavenly Father.

“Be as a father unto the fatherless, and instead of an husband unto their mother.” That is the opposite of the mindset of a whoremonger, who asks, what can I do to this sister, how can I take advantage of this single mother? The son of the Most High asks, what can I do for this young man to build him up? That is why Bishop Nathanyel says it is easier to build up a young man, a child, than to fix a broken old man; the broken old man is the one looking to take advantage.

“So shalt thou be as the son of the most High.” If you go opposite of that, you cannot be the son of the Most High. If you are looking at this sister with lustful eyes, trying to figure out how to get in her pants or take advantage of her, you can’t be the son of the Most High, and wisdom cannot dwell in you.

That is the charge on the friend of God and the prophet: to go out and raise up God’s children, which is why he cannot walk in hypocrisy. Much is given to you, and much is going to be required of you.

Galatians 3:10 says, “For as many as are of the works of the law are under the curse: for it is written, Cursed is every one that continueth not in all things which are written in the book of the law to do them.” Deuteronomy 27 is where Paul is quoting from.

“Cursed be the man that maketh any graven or molten image, an abomination unto the Lord, the work of the hands of the craftsman, and putteth it in a secret place. And all the people shall answer and say, Amen.” That is death, and we agreed to it: break these commandments and we would be destroyed. Then it goes down the list. “Cursed be he that setteth light by his father or his mother”, that is, dishonours them. Cursed be he that removeth his neighbour's landmark, that maketh the blind to wander, that perverteth the judgment of the stranger, fatherless, and widow, that lieth with his father's wife. “Cursed be he that lieth with any manner of beast”: no animal atones for that. Cursed be he that lieth with his sister or his mother in law, that smiteth his neighbour secretly, that “taketh reward to slay an innocent person.” And every time, all the people said Amen. They agreed to being cursed if they violated these laws.

Then the last: “Cursed be he that confirmeth not all the words of this law to do them. And all the people shall say, Amen.” That is the line Paul quotes. All these things go into morality, civil and moral law, dealing with your brother, your father, your sister; it goes right back to loving thy neighbour as thyself.

That is the curse. Idolatry, adultery, murder, bestiality: there was no repentance and no animal in the temple that could atone for them. The Galatians, the northern kingdom and the scattered Israelites, were heavily rooted in idolatry, so under the old covenant they were immediately condemned. That is why Paul asks whether they received the Spirit by the works of the law. If you are under that law of sacrifice, you are under the curse, because what you are guilty of cannot be atoned for under Mosaic law. They came into the faith hearing that Christ had died for them and redeemed them from sins the animals could never cover.

Galatians 3:11 says, “But that no man is justified by the law in the sight of God, it is evident: for, The just shall live by faith.” The law that cannot justify is the law of sacrifice. Paul is quoting Habakkuk 2:4.

“Behold, his soul which is lifted up is not upright in him”. That is Esau. His soul is not right by spirit, by nature, by biology; that nation is not right at all in the spirit or in their heads. “but the just shall live by his faith.” That is where Paul got it.

Abraham's faith was counted for righteousness, and his faith came first, before his works; then his works proved his faith, because they go hand in hand. So the just shall live by faith, and that faith is faith in Christ. The just are those keeping God's laws, the law that is holy, just and good, and they live by faith in Christ, not by the blood of animals.

Caiaphas points out what the curse of the law is. “And one of them, named Caiaphas, being the high priest that same year, said unto them, Ye know nothing at all, Nor consider that it is expedient for us, that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation perish not.”

Why would the whole nation perish? Because they were under the old covenant that they agreed to and kept violating over and over again. The northern kingdom went off first, and the southern kingdom fell right after, and both were destroyed by the nations. Standing in the old covenant, based on our own actions and on the law and the prophets, both kingdoms were condemned. By default both were under the curse of the law, which is condemnation. They should have been destroyed.

But the Lord had other plans. He said, I will not destroy them; I love them; I am going to have my son go and die for them, and redeem them from the curse they agreed to in Deuteronomy 27, where all the people said Amen. That is Galatians 3:13: “Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us”. The curse and death are the same thing; being made a curse for us means he was killed for us. Christ died to take us out of that contract and put us into a new one, “That the blessing of Abraham might come on the Gentiles through Jesus Christ”, the northern kingdom.

What makes you just, so that you live by faith? “Wherefore the law is holy, and the commandment holy, and just, and good.” The law is holy, and the commandment is holy and just and good.

So when you are just, what are you keeping? God's laws. And what will you live by? Faith in Christ. That is what Habakkuk is talking about when he says the just shall live by his faith, and that is what Paul is talking about in Galatians 3:11. The just are those who keep God's commandments, and they shall live by faith.

So Paul is not throwing away the commandments. The law that cannot justify is the law of sacrifice; the commandments are what make a man just, and the just man lives by faith in Christ.

Just in case Isaiah 27 is not enough, beat a dead horse. “And it shall come to pass in that day, that the Lord shall set his hand again the second time to recover the remnant of his people.” That is the same gathering we read in Isaiah 27.

From where? “Which shall be left, from Assyria”: my people. “And from Egypt”: Egypt, my people. “And from Pathros”: still Egypt, my people. “And from Cush, and from Elam”: Elam is Iran and Pakistan, my people. “And from Shinar”: Shinar is Iraq, my people. “And from Hamath”: Syria, my people. “And from the islands of the sea”: the islands, whether the Mediterranean or the Caribbean. That is his people.

It names Assyria and Egypt right there with the rest, and in every one of those places it is the remnant of his people that he recovers, not the nations of those lands. So when Isaiah 19 says “Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands”, it is speaking of Israel scattered in Egypt and Assyria, whom the Lord recovers the second time.

“Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel mine inheritance.” That is the one verse they might run with: see, Egypt is his people and Assyria is his people, so the Egyptians and the Assyrians are saved too. No problem. Go over a few chapters and see where this Egypt and Assyria are.

“And it shall come to pass in that day, that the Lord shall beat off from the channel of the river unto the stream of Egypt, and ye shall be gathered one by one, O ye children of Israel.” Gathered one by one: who? The children of Israel.

“And it shall come to pass in that day, that the great trumpet shall be blown”: that is Christ coming. “And they shall come which were ready to perish in the land of Assyria, and the outcasts in the land of Egypt.” Earlier it said Egypt and Assyria; here it is the land of Assyria and the land of Egypt, and the ones coming out of them are the children of Israel. So who is “Egypt my people” and Assyria? Israelites.

“And shall worship the Lord in the holy mount at Jerusalem.” My people in Egypt and my people in Assyria means Israel in those lands, scattered there and gathered out one by one to worship at Jerusalem. That is how precepts work: you don't build a doctrine for another nation on one verse.

One more, just in case. “And I will strengthen the house of Judah, and I will save the house of Joseph, and I will bring them again to place them.” Bring them again: that is the second time, the recovering of Isaiah 11. “For I have mercy upon them: and they shall be as though I had not cast them off”: as though they had never been in captivity. “For I am the Lord their God, and will hear them.”

“And they of Ephraim shall be like a mighty man, and their heart shall rejoice as through wine: yea, their children shall see it, and be glad.” “I will hiss for them, and gather them; for I have redeemed them.” Both Judah and Joseph, Judah and Ephraim: he will gather all twelve tribes. “And they shall increase as they have increased. And I will sow them among the people: and they shall remember me in far countries; and they shall live with their children, and turn again.”

“I will bring them again also out of the land of Egypt, and gather them out of Assyria.” Bring who again? All twelve tribes, out of Egypt and out of Assyria, the same as Isaiah 11:11. “And I will bring them into the land of Gilead and Lebanon; and place shall not be found for them.”

So what does “Egypt my people” and “Assyria the work of my hands” mean? It means Israel in those lands. That makes four scriptures, and there is no arguing with it. That is called precepts.

Saul disobeyed a direct order, and through Samuel the Lord asks him a question: “Hath the Lord as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the Lord?” Answer it.

“Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams.” The Lord cared about obedience more than animal sacrifices.

That is the same point as Mark 12:33, that loving God and your neighbour “is more than all whole burnt offerings and sacrifices.” Saul wanted to bring the sacrifice after he had disobeyed; Israel wanted to bring the best animal after they had wronged their neighbour. The Lord wants the obedience. And that is why James 2 holds us to the royal law, love thy neighbour as thyself, and not to an offering that covers over a sin against the brother.

“Therefore have I hewed them by the prophets; I have slain them by the words of my mouth.” The word of God can slay; it is the spirit. “And thy judgments are as the light that goeth forth.”

“For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.” He was not about the sacrifice. That was a schoolmaster, a placeholder. He desired mercy and the knowledge of God.

The Lord eventually said away with it, through the prophets themselves. And that is where James 2:13 lands: “For he shall have judgment without mercy, that hath shewed no mercy; and mercy rejoiceth against judgment.” You shall receive no mercy if you show no mercy. Mercy rejoices against judgment: the Most High chooses to have mercy rather than to judge you for violating the royal law, and he looks for that same mercy in us toward our neighbour.

“For all sacrifice is too little for a sweet savour unto thee, and all the fat is not sufficient for thy burnt offering: but he that feareth the Lord is great at all times.”

All sacrifice is too little. He that fears the Lord is great at all times. The Lord is saying, sacrificing, I don’t care about that; fearing me and obeying me is more important.

That closes the line of scriptures: Mark 12:33, Ecclesiasticus 35, 1 Samuel 15:22, Psalms 40:6, Proverbs 21:3, Hosea 6:6 and Judith 16:16 all say the same thing. Then back to James 2. “For whosoever shall keep the whole law, and yet offend in one point, he is guilty of all.” Christians use this to say that if you sin in one law you break them all, so you can’t keep them at all. But the context is the royal law, love your neighbour as yourself, and James explains it himself: “For he that said, Do not commit adultery, said also, Do not kill.” If you commit no adultery but you kill your brother, you are a transgressor of the royal law.

“So speak ye, and so do, as they that shall be judged by the law of liberty.” Under the old covenant, if you violated the moral law, moved your neighbour’s landmark or slept with your brother’s wife, you got death. Christ redeemed us from that and put us under the law of liberty. So stop doing it.

Mark gives the same account with more detail, and it ties into sacrifice. “And one of the scribes came.” In Matthew he is called a lawyer; in Mark he is called a scribe, because they wrote things over and over and had the law in their minds. There were a bunch of them, but he was bold and spoke up: “Which is the first commandment of all?”

“The first of all the commandments is, Hear, O Israel; The Lord our God is one Lord”: that is Deuteronomy 6:4. “And thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind, and with all thy strength: this is the first commandment.” The commandments, the dietary law, the civil law, the sacrificial law, all of that is in there. “And the second is like, namely this, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. There is none other commandment greater than these.” If you can keep those, you can keep them all.

“Well, Master, thou hast said the truth”: true, true, true. Then verse 33: “to love him with all the heart, and with all the understanding, and with all the soul, and with all the strength, and to love his neighbour as himself, is more than all whole burnt offerings and sacrifices.” It is better than sacrifices. That is why Mark is loved: he makes it clear.

Why is it more than sacrifices? Because Israel would mess around, offer sacrifices, and then hate their neighbour, kill their neighbour, steal from their neighbour, bang their neighbour’s wife or sleep with their neighbour’s husband, but offer the best animal. The Lord said, I don’t care about that stuff. I care about your obedience, loving each other, loving me above the animals.

“But when the Pharisees had heard that he had put the Sadducees to silence, they were gathered together.” Christ had put the Sadducees to shame, and the Pharisees saw how sharp he was. “Then one of them, which was a lawyer, asked him a question, tempting him.”

A lawyer is a scribe. Their job was writing the Bible over and over again, because ink fades and animal skin and paper rip and smear, so it had to be copied again and again. They were the recorders and copyists, and they knew the law and the prophets off top. That is why he was tempting Christ: he already knew the answer. “Master, which is the great commandment in the law?”

“Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind. This is the first and great commandment.” That is the first four of the ten spoken commandments. “And the second is like unto it, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.” That is the six, the royal law of James 2:8.

“On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets.” These two are an abbreviation of all the laws. Loving God with all your heart, soul and mind means keeping the Sabbath day holy, the Passover, Tabernacles, Pentecost, the new moons, keeping the congregation, and the dietary law: don’t drink blood, don’t eat pork or shrimp. That is all serving God. The ten are an umbrella over all of them.

“To do justice and judgment is more acceptable to the Lord than sacrifice.”

To do justice and judgment, just like the Lord told Saul to do, is more acceptable than sacrifice. He says it over and over and over again: in Samuel, in the Psalms, in Mark, and here in Proverbs.

Justice and judgment is how you treat your neighbour. In James 2 the assembly seated the rich man in a good place and told the poor man to stand there, and James asks, “Are ye not then partial in yourselves, and are become judges of evil thoughts?” That is the opposite of doing justice and judgment, and no sacrifice would make up for it. Keeping the royal law is what is acceptable to the Lord.

“Sacrifice and offering thou didst not desire; mine ears hast thou opened: burnt offering and sin offering hast thou not required.” This is quoted again in Hebrews 10.

David is saying, you opened my ears, and I understand the spirit: you don’t really care about sacrifices. Remember David wanted to build the temple. But the spirit was revealed to him that the sacrifices were just a placeholder for Christ to show up. He learned that because Christ was speaking through him.

So David realized: you don’t care about sacrifices at all, you care about obedience. That is what Samuel told Saul when he was king, “to obey is better than sacrifice.” And it is why the royal law of James 2, loving the neighbour and not being a respecter of persons, is what God is looking for.

James 2:8 says “If ye fulfil the royal law according to the scripture, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself, ye do well.” What is the royal law? Romans 13 lays it out.

“Owe no man any thing, but to love one another: for he that loveth another hath fulfilled the law.” What law? Love your neighbour as yourself. “For this, Thou shalt not commit adultery, Thou shalt not kill, Thou shalt not steal, Thou shalt not bear false witness, Thou shalt not covet”: every one of those is the royal law. “And if there be any other commandment”, any other commandment regarding your neighbour outside of those, “it is briefly comprehended in this saying, namely, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.”

Love your neighbour as yourself is an abbreviation of the six commandments. Of the ten spoken commandments, the first four are how you observe God, and the last six are how you serve your neighbour: honour your father and mother, don’t commit adultery, don’t kill, don’t steal, don’t bear false witness, don’t covet. Those six are briefly comprehended in that one saying. The ten spoken commandments were themselves an abbreviation.

“Love worketh no ill to his neighbour”: no ill like being a respecter of persons, seating the man with the gold ring in a good place and telling the poor man to stand over there. “Therefore love is the fulfilling of the law.” Do we keep it? Yes, you simple Christians. That is the royal law James is talking about, and respect of persons is sin against it.

Mark 12:33 said loving God and your neighbour is more than all whole burnt offerings and sacrifices. Ecclesiasticus 35 says the same.

“He that keepeth the law bringeth offerings enough: he that taketh heed to the commandment offereth a peace offering.” Keeping the law is offering enough.

“He that requiteth a good turn offereth fine flour.” Under the offerings, you offered an animal, or fine flour if you were poor. Here, requiting a good turn, which is loving your neighbour as yourself, is the fine flour. “And he that giveth alms sacrificeth praise.”

“To depart from wickedness is a thing pleasing to the Lord; and to forsake unrighteousness is a propitiation.” Propitiation means mercy, reconciliation. Departing from wickedness toward your neighbour is what reconciles you to God, which is why the royal law of James 2:8 stands above the sacrifices.

“And Abraham was ninety years old and nine, when he was circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin.” “And Ishmael his son was thirteen years old, when he was circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin.”

Abraham was not circumcised on the eighth day after he was born; he was ninety-nine. Ishmael was thirteen. There was no eighth day, no days of purifying and no sacrifice. That is circumcision of the fathers, not circumcision after the manner of Moses.

The Pharisees wanted circumcision and sacrifice together, after the manner of Moses, because sacrificing was their bread and butter. As more people followed Christ, more of them stopped sacrificing, and if the people stop sacrificing, the Pharisees cannot eat. So they went into the churches saying you have to be circumcised to be saved. That is not what the Bible, Christ or the apostles taught. They were trying to put back on the people the yoke that could not be borne, the same one Peter asked about: “why tempt ye God, to put a yoke upon the neck of the disciples, which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear?”

“And the Lord visited Sarah as he had said”, and “Sarah conceived, and bare Abraham a son in his old age, at the set time of which God had spoken to him.” Sarah conceived in old age and Abraham named the child Isaac. Then: “And Abraham circumcised his son Isaac being eight days old, as God had commanded him.” “And Abraham was an hundred years old, when his son Isaac was born unto him.”

Isaac was circumcised on the eighth day, as God commanded, but this was long before Moses. There is no reading of them going and sacrificing animals for it. So even eighth-day circumcision here is not after the manner of Moses. There is circumcision of the fathers, and there is circumcision after the manner of Moses, which carries the sacrifice.

That is how Paul can say in Galatians 5, “if ye be circumcised, Christ shall profit you nothing.” He means circumcised after the manner of Moses, back under the yoke of bondage, taught by the Pharisees that you must be circumcised and sacrifice an animal to be saved. “For I testify again to every man that is circumcised, that he is a debtor to do the whole law.” Once the temple was destroyed and the priests scattered, that man had no way to keep it and was finished.

“Christ is become of no effect unto you, whosoever of you are justified by the law; ye are fallen from grace.” Christ's sacrifice does away with the animal sacrifice, so whoever runs back to animals to atone for sin rejects what Christ did on the cross. Paul is not throwing out the commandments. He is rejecting the sacrifice that was bewitching the Galatians. So “Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage.”

If circumcision after the manner of Moses is circumcision with sacrifice, is all circumcision of Moses? Christ answers it: “Moses therefore gave unto you circumcision; (not because it is of Moses, but of the fathers;) and ye on the sabbath day circumcise a man.”

Moses gave it to them, but circumcision is not of Moses. It is of the fathers, of Abraham, who was the one first circumcised. So when Acts 15 says circumcised after the manner of Moses, that is not the same thing as the circumcision of Abraham.

There are two different things here: circumcision of the fathers, and circumcision after the manner of Moses with the sacrifice of Leviticus 12 behind it. Seeing that difference is what opens up what the Pharisees were demanding and what Paul was fighting in his letters.

In Acts 15 certain men came down from Judea and taught, “Except ye be circumcised after the manner of Moses, ye cannot be saved.” Why does it say after the manner of Moses and not just circumcision? Leviticus 12 shows the manner of Moses. A woman who “conceived seed, and born a man child” is unclean seven days; “in the eighth day the flesh of his foreskin shall be circumcised”; she continues in the blood of her purifying thirty-three more days, forty in all for a boy and eighty for a girl. When the days are fulfilled she brings a lamb and a pigeon or turtledove for a burnt offering and a sin offering, and if she cannot afford a lamb, “two turtles, or two young pigeons”. The priest makes the atonement, and the offering covers the child as well as the mother.

Luke 2 confirms it with Mary and Christ. Mary conceived seed and bore a man child. “And when eight days were accomplished for the circumcising of the child, his name was called JESUS, which was so named of the angel before he was conceived in the womb.” That is the eighth day of Leviticus 12.

“And when the days of her purification according to the law of Moses were accomplished, they brought him to Jerusalem, to present him to the Lord”, because “Every male that openeth the womb shall be called holy to the Lord”. Then comes the offering: “to offer a sacrifice according to that which is said in the law of the Lord, A pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons.” Those are the offerings Leviticus 12:8 names.

So behind circumcision after the manner of Moses comes sacrifice. It is circumcision with the eighth day, the days of purifying and the offering for the woman and the child all tied together. That is what the men from Judea were pressing on the Gentiles, and that is why the scripture calls it the manner of Moses.

God told Isaac why the promise stood: “Because that Abraham obeyed my voice, and kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws.” Abraham obeyed, and he kept the charge, the commandments, the statutes and the laws. That is past tense. It tells you what Abraham was doing from the beginning that proved his faith. His obedience was his acceptable faithfulness, the performance of Sirach 15:15.

Paul writes, “And the law is not of faith: but, The man that doeth them shall live in them.” The law meant there is the law of sacrifice, which came later. Abraham's faith came first, and his faith and the promise to him go hand in hand; the promise predates the law of sacrifice.

“Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us”. The curse of the law is condemnation, not being able to atone for every sin. Caiaphas pointed it out without knowing it: “it is expedient for us, that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation perish not.” Both the northern and southern kingdoms were under the old covenant they agreed to in Deuteronomy 27 and kept breaking, so both were condemned and destroyed by the nations. But the Lord loved them, sent his son to die for them, and took them out of that contract into a new one, “That the blessing of Abraham might come on the Gentiles through Jesus Christ”, meaning the northern kingdom.

Paul says “before faith came, we were kept under the law”, and “the law was our schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ, that we might be justified by faith.” The schoolmaster is the law of sacrifice, and the “we” is Israel. After faith came, “we are no longer under a schoolmaster.” Jews, Greeks, bond, free, male and female were all the same people of God in Christ.

“And if ye be Christ’s, then are ye Abraham’s seed, and heirs according to the promise.” Abraham is the father of faith, so his children should be children of faith like him: keeping the commandments the way he did, with faith in Christ instead of the animal sacrifice the Galatians were bewitched back into. The promise pertains to the Israelites, not to all nations.

Sirach 15:15 says, “If thou wilt, to keep the commandments, and to perform acceptable faithfulness.” Keeping God's commandments is performing acceptable faithfulness: those are your actions, and that is where your faith lies. Your works prove your faith and your faith proves your works; they go hand in hand. God “hath set fire and water before thee: stretch forth thy hand unto whether thou wilt.”

For anyone still confused, Sirach 19:20 says it again: “The fear of the Lord is all wisdom; and in all wisdom is the performance of the law, and the knowledge of his omnipotency.” The performance of the law is the acceptable faithfulness of Sirach 15. Wisdom is not only knowing the law; it is performing it.

The words “the knowledge of his omnipotency” mean knowing that God is all around us, and we acknowledge it by keeping his laws.

This is what Habakkuk and Paul mean by the just living by faith. Paul says “the law is holy, and the commandment holy, and just, and good.” The just are those who keep God's laws and commandments, and they live by faith in Christ. Fearing God, keeping his law and living by faith are one walk.
