That same serpent spirit is still speaking. Christ told the Pharisees, “Ye are of your father the devil,” “a liar, and the father of it.” The serpent seed came through Cain, and it lives on in Esau, the so-called white man, the pioneer of lying, who persuades the world today through his media and his religion. It is a battle for the minds of the people, and the answer is to stay in the word.

Genesis 5 traces the lineage from Adam down to Noah, who “begat Shem, Ham, and Japheth.” Then Genesis 6 says “the sons of God saw the daughters of men that they were fair.” The sons of God are that lineage just named; the daughters of men are the daughters of the other nations that were created. These are not literal angels. The chapter before gives the understanding, and the scriptures that follow prove who the sons of God are.

John writes it in the New Testament: “Behold, what manner of love the Father hath bestowed upon us, that we should be called the sons of God.” That is what God calls us. Brothers, you are walking gods, whoever gets upset about it, the apologists included.

“therefore the world knoweth us not, because it knew him not.” The world looks at our people, calls us Negroes, and refuses to believe these could be the people of the book, the sons of God. And it knew him not: to this day they refuse to say Christ was a black man. They put the image of Cesare Borgia in every church, comic book and piece of media, while the Bible says he is black, of the tribe of Judah.

So when Genesis 6 speaks of “the sons of God” going in to the daughters of men, it is speaking of the same people John calls the sons of God: Adam’s line, our forefathers.

Baruch says the same thing as Genesis 6: “There were the giants famous from the beginning, that were of so great stature, and so expert in war.” Those giants were the offspring of the sons of God, the mighty men of renown, and they were expert in war as well.

“Those did not the Lord choose, neither gave he the way of knowledge unto them.” God did not choose them; they were wicked. “But they were destroyed, because they had no wisdom, and perished through their own foolishness.” How were they destroyed? The flood. God saw that “every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually,” and he wiped it out.

But those same spirits came right back, by way of the three sons of Noah, Shem, Ham and Japheth. There is no new thing under the sun. Jude speaks of “certain men crept in unawares, who were before of old ordained to this condemnation,” the same words, “of old,” that Genesis 6 uses of the men of renown. The same kind of wickedness is still here, reserved “unto the judgment of the great day,” which has not yet come.

So the giants are not a fantasy of fallen angels, the Nephilim Esau talks about. They were men, the offspring of the sons of God, who had no wisdom, and whose spirit lives on until the judgment.

The sons of God in Genesis 6 are Adam’s line, the lineage traced in Genesis 5. Did that name change later, after the flood and after Egypt? No. Deuteronomy 14:1, spoken after the Exodus, says to Israel: “Ye are the children of the Lord your God.”

We are the children of the Lord our God because we are the sons of God. The same people carried the same title from Adam through Noah, through the fathers, out of Egypt, and into the law.

This matters for reading Genesis 6 rightly. The sons of God who went in to the daughters of men were not angels coming down from the sky; they were men of that same chosen line, God’s own children, who mixed with the other nations when it was forbidden. That sin brought the flood, and later the affliction of our people. The scriptures do not change the name: from Genesis, to Deuteronomy, to the prophets, to the New Testament, it is our people who are called the children and the sons of God.

The title “sons of God” runs through the whole book. After Deuteronomy called Israel “the children of the Lord your God,” did anything change in the prophets? No. Hosea 1:10: “Yet the number of the children of Israel shall be as the sand of the sea, which cannot be measured nor numbered.”

“And it shall come to pass, that in the place where it was said unto them, Ye are not my people.” That place is where our people are today: America and the diaspora, Jamaica, Haiti, Africa, Europe. Everywhere we were told we are not God’s people. “there it shall be said unto them, Ye are the sons of the living God.”

God calls us the sons of the living God. That is who we are. So the sons of God of Genesis 6 are the same nation the prophet speaks of: the children of Israel, scattered and counted as nothing, yet still his sons. The world does not know us, but God does, and in the very place where we were called not his people, he will call us his sons again.

Genesis 6:4 says the children of the sons of God and the daughters of men “became mighty men which were of old, men of renown,” and that “There were giants in the earth in those days.” Judith’s song names that kind of people: “For the mighty one did not fall by the young men, neither did the sons of the Titans smite him, nor high giants set upon him: but Judith the daughter of Merari weakened him with the beauty of her countenance.”

The sons of the Titans and the high giants are those giants, the men of renown of Genesis 6, the offspring of the sons of God.

That is where Esau gets his Titan movies, and his Greek mythology of Hercules and the half-gods. He always mixes some lies in with the truth. He tells those stories because he looks at us as gods: because of our DNA, our physical prowess, our melanin. We are the sons of God, demigods on the earth, and that is why when our people are put into sports or anything physical, we dominate. Everybody wants our rhythm, but nobody wants our blues.

So the Titans of the Greek stories are not fallen angels or gods of another people. They are a twisted memory of the mighty men born when the sons of God went in to the daughters of men.

“the sons of God saw the daughters of men” in Genesis 6 is about men, not spirits; God says “My spirit shall not always strive with man, for that he also is flesh.” Psalms 82:6 shows who these sons of God are and what God calls them: “I have said, Ye are gods; and all of you are children of the most High.”

We are gods, and we are children of the Most High. That is why the sons of God in Genesis 6 are called by that name: they carried that DNA, made in the image of God.

It is also why their sin was so serious. Back in Genesis 6:4, “There were giants in the earth in those days; and also after that, when the sons of God came in unto the daughters of men.” The sons of God, the children of the Most High, took wives of the other nations, which was forbidden. The children born to them “became mighty men which were of old, men of renown,” and “God saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually.” So the Most High brought destruction, and later we had to pay for what we did as the sons of God; he told Abraham his seed would be afflicted in a land not theirs for four hundred years.

Daniel shows again what heaven means: “And the kingdom and dominion, and the greatness of the kingdom under the whole heaven, shall be given to the people of the saints of the most High.” That is rulership. The greatness of the kingdom under the whole heaven is dominion over the nations, and it is given to the saints of the Most High, Israel.

So when Isaiah says “How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning! how art thou cut down to the ground, which didst weaken the nations!”, it is the fall of a ruler from his dominion. How did you fall from rulership? Lucifer is the king of Babylon, the oppressor who weakened the nations with his bombs, his lies and his fornication.

He said in his heart, “I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of God: I will sit also upon the mount of the congregation, in the sides of the north”, North America, and “I will be like the most High.” “Yet thou shalt be brought down to hell, to the sides of the pit.”

Put the two together. The rulership he grasped at, he loses, and the kingdom and dominion under the whole heaven is given to the people of the saints of the Most High. It is not an angel cast out of the sky; it is the man, this so-called white man, America, brought down, and Israel lifted up to rule.

“How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer”: before we can know who Lucifer is, we have to know what heaven is. Lamentations shows it: “How hath the Lord covered the daughter of Zion with a cloud in his anger, and cast down from heaven unto the earth the beauty of Israel.”

Heaven is dominion and rulership. That was the high standard, the high estate Israel held, and the beauty of Israel was cast down from it to the earth. We were set down to a low state. No one thinks Israel was literally thrown out of the sky; we fell from rulership.

So it is with Lucifer. Esau takes Jude and Isaiah 14, mixes them up and comes with this fallen angel teaching. But keep it in context. Lucifer, the lightbearer, is the king of Babylon of verse 4, the oppressor, the one who “smote the people in wrath with a continual stroke.” It is talking about a nation: this so-called white man, America, whom everybody looks at as god and all knowing because he controls communication everywhere.

He is falling from heaven the same way Israel did: he is losing his dominion and his rulership. “They that see thee shall narrowly look upon thee, and consider thee, saying, Is this the man that made the earth to tremble”: not a fallen angel, not the Nephilim, but the man, the one who made the earth tremble by dropping atom bombs everywhere. The angels are not falling out of heaven; they take their directive from the Most High God.

Christ “will destroy in this mountain the face of the covering cast over all people.” Somebody might ask, what mountain is this? Mount Ararat, Mount Fuji, Mount Kilimanjaro? No. Isaiah 13 shows it: “The burden of Babylon, which Isaiah the son of Amoz did see.” That is Babylon the great.

“Lift ye up a banner upon the high mountain.” That high mountain is America. God says lift up the banner, and the banner is the Bible. “exalt the voice unto them”: that is what we do every day, every time we go to camp and every time we do these classes, casting down lies. “shake the hand”: rebuke them. “that they may go into the gates of the nobles.”

So the mountain of Isaiah 25:7 is Babylon the great, America, and the covering cast over all people is spread from there. It is not only over the people in America; it is global. Wherever you go, whatever church you sit in, whatever continent, country or island, they all think the white man is God and that Christ is white. Now the same persuasion is being pushed that the UFOs, the chariots, are demonic fallen angels, to turn the minds of the people to fight against Christ.

How did he spread this veil over all nations? His media, his network, his communication, because he is the prince of the power of the air; he controls the airwaves. And how will the covering be destroyed? The Most High is using us to do it: lifting up the banner, the Bible, upon that high mountain, exalting the voice, casting down the lies and revealing the lies Esau has been telling our people.

In Job, “the sons of God came to present themselves before the Lord, and Satan came also among them. And the Lord said unto Satan, Whence comest thou?” But I thought he got kicked out of heaven and was one of the fallen ones? No. He is there because he works for God. God created good angels and bad angels, and Satan’s job is to tempt us; he is only allowed to do what God allows. The prophet Micaiah saw the same court of heaven.

“I saw the Lord sitting on his throne, and all the host of heaven standing by him on his right hand and on his left.” The angels on the right hand go forth for righteousness, and the ones on the left go forth for evil, for judgment.

“And the Lord said, Who shall persuade Ahab, that he may go up and fall at Ramoth–gilead?” One said one thing and another said another. “And there came forth a spirit, and stood before the Lord, and said, I will persuade him.” “I will go forth, and I will be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets. And he said, Thou shalt persuade him, and prevail also: go forth, and do so.”

God gave that spirit the authority to do it, the same way he gave Satan the authority in Job 1 to tempt Job: destroy everything, but do not touch Job himself. Even the lying spirit stands before the throne and goes out only when the Lord sends it. That is why the fallen angel doctrine is crap, and why it is a shame to hear black pastors, not only Edomite pastors, repeating that same garbage rhetoric and defiling the minds of the people.

This shows how the angels do what the Most High tells them. “There be spirits that are created for vengeance, which in their fury lay on sore strokes; in the time of destruction they pour out their force, and appease the wrath of him that made them.” Those are the angels on the left hand of God, and they minister unto God and to us.

“Fire, and hail, and famine, and death, all these were created for vengeance; Teeth of wild beasts, and scorpions, serpents, and the sword punishing the wicked to destruction.”

Here is the point: “They shall rejoice in his commandment, and they shall be ready upon earth, when need is; and when their time is come, they shall not transgress his word.” They do what God tells them to do. They do not have free will to say, let’s go down and sleep with some human women today. That is not what goes on in the heavens.

So when Satan went forth to touch all that Job had, he was doing what God allowed and no more. Even the spirits made for vengeance do not transgress his word.

The psalm calls the angels “ministers of his, that do his pleasure.” They minister unto the Most High, but they minister unto us as well: “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent forth to minister for them who shall be heirs of salvation?”

Who is going to be heir of salvation? Us, if we keep the commandments. So the angels work on our behalf. They are ministering spirits, sent forth by God for his people.

So the angels that come before the Lord in Job 1 are not rebels running loose. They are sent forth at his word, whether to try a man like Job or to minister for the heirs of salvation.

“Bless the Lord, ye his angels, that excel in strength, that do his commandments, hearkening unto the voice of his word.” That do his commandments. I thought he kicked them out of heaven because they were disobedient and tried to overthrow him, and now they are fallen? No: they do his commandments. We just read about the spirit sent forth in 1 Kings 22, and about Satan working for the Most High in Job 1. The angels hearken unto the voice of the Most High.

“Bless ye the Lord, all ye his hosts; ye ministers of his, that do his pleasure.” Keep that word ministers in mind. They minister unto the Most High, doing his pleasure, and they also minister unto us.

“Bless the Lord, all his works in all places of his dominion: bless the Lord, O my soul.” Every angel in every place of his dominion is under his rule, carrying out his commandments, which is why Satan could only go as far as the Lord allowed him with Job.

The angels minister unto the Most High, and they minister unto us. “The angel of the Lord encampeth round about them that fear him, and delivereth them.” These are the good angels. They encamp around them that fear him and deliver them from all evil, like it says in the Lord’s prayer.

Our forefathers never looked at the angels as some demonic thing that came down to earth to persecute and kill them. When three men stood by Abraham in the plains of Mamre, he ran to meet them, bowed himself, had water fetched to wash their feet and prepared a calf for them to eat. When two angels came to Sodom, Lot rose up to meet them, bowed with his face to the ground and made them a feast, and they did eat. They look like us.

The angel in Revelation told John, I am thy fellow servant and of thy brethren; the angels have tribes too. Raphael presented the prayers of the saints. They are our brothers, working on our behalf. Calling them demons and fallen angels is Esau’s popular persuasion. The angel of the Lord camps round about them that fear God, just as the Lord set a hedge about Job, and delivers them.
blog/2026/2026-05-16-2026-05-16-the-bold:
Saul finally confessed in verse 24: “I have sinned: for I have transgressed the commandment of the Lord, and thy words: because I feared the people, and obeyed their voice.” If you are a leader and you are in fear of your people, or you don’t want them to be mad at you, what can those people do to you? Manipulate you. You are a pushover; they can sway you to the left and to the right. Who is supposed to move you? The Lord, not the people you are supposed to lead. You are not leading the people; you are being led by the people.

Then verse 28: “And Samuel said unto him, The Lord hath rent the kingdom of Israel from thee this day, and hath given it to a neighbour of thine, that is better than thou.” Damn.

That is what the bashful spirit costs. Verse 23 already said it: “Because thou hast rejected the word of the Lord, he hath also rejected thee from being king.” When you are in that spirit the Lord can’t use you; you are not a good leader. Leadership may see something in you and put you in a position, and then when we question you on certain things you make excuses, or you separate yourself into a bubble with the men under you. You are bashful, you are bringing up a bunch of bashful brothers under you, and you are keeping the brothers under you hostage.

The Lord had made Saul king “When thou wast little in thine own sight”, when he thought he was a nobody. And because he feared the people and would not obey, the kingdom was torn from him and given to his neighbour, David, who was better than he.

What is going on in 1 Samuel 15? The Lord commanded Saul to utterly destroy all the Amalekites and everything they have, every last one of them. The Lord told Saul, wipe these devils out. And he didn’t do it.

The commandment was total: “Now go and smite Amalek, and utterly destroy all that they have, and spare them not; but slay both man and woman, infant and suckling, ox and sheep, camel and ass.” All that they have. All means everything.

Now hold that against Saul’s answer in verse 20: “Yea, I have obeyed the voice of the Lord, and have gone the way which the Lord sent me, and have brought Agag the king of Amalek, and have utterly destroyed the Amalekites.” Wait a minute: the king is still alive. What do you mean you followed the commandment of the Lord? Saul is playing the defensive, justifying himself, making excuses.

Then verse 21: “But the people took of the spoil, sheep and oxen, the chief of the things which should have been utterly destroyed, to sacrifice unto the Lord thy God in Gilgal.” It wasn’t me, it was the people, it was their fault; I couldn’t do nothing about it. That is bashfulness: you don’t take accountability. The commandment said spare the sheep and oxen not, and Saul brought them back and blamed the people.

So Samuel answered, “to obey is better than sacrifice.” To do what you were told is better than coming back saying, my bad, I thought I understood what you wanted, I decided to do it this way. You fulfill the commandment you were given, and if there is a problem, you say something.

“For we walk by faith, not by sight.” Christians use that all the time and don’t know what it means. But in this aspect we can use it about fear.

We fear what we see. We don’t fear the Lord; we fear what we physically see. A brother at camp gets unruly with us, he’s got a gun or a knife or whatever, and we fear that. But we don’t fear breaking God’s commandments. That we don’t really fear.

That was Saul. When he “saw the host of the Philistines, he was afraid.” He walked by sight. He feared the Philistines he could see and the people who were scattering from him, but he did not fear transgressing the commandment of the Lord, and it cost him the kingdom.

“For God hath not given us the spirit of fear.” The Bible says the Lord never gave us that spirit. So the fear Saul had when his heart greatly trembled goes back into a lack of faith.

“But of power, and of love, and of a sound mind.” We are supposed to have the spirit of power, love and a sound mind.

“Be not thou therefore ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, nor of me his prisoner: but be thou partaker of the afflictions of the gospel according to the power of God.” We are not supposed to be ashamed of the testimony of Christ. The bashful brother is ashamed and afraid; the one who has God’s spirit partakes of the afflictions of the gospel by the power of God.

“And when Saul saw the host of the Philistines, he was afraid, and his heart greatly trembled.” He was scared. This is the king. If the king is scared, what is that going to do to the men under him? If the officer is fearful, what is that going to do to the soldiers under him? It is going to spread.

“As the judge of the people is himself, so are his officers”: so are they that are under him. “And what manner of man the ruler of the city is, such are all they that dwell therein.” Whatever man the ruler is, like King Saul, such are all that dwell under him.

Take an example. Some brothers have been here six months, a year maybe, not long, still in regular clothes. Some officers have been here eight, nine, ten years. Those young men in the regular shirts are going to follow the example of the officers in the purple shirts. So if you are bashful, afraid, timid and shy, what does that communicate to them spiritually? That they can be timid, shy, fearful and bashful too. You don’t have to say nothing; your spirit is telling them, it’s okay to be like this, the officer can be fearful and timid, so I’ll follow his example, now I know how to move around in here.

It shall not be so. It shall not be so in here.

“And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul.” This is the level we have to get to: where we are not afraid of those brothers and sisters, and the other nations, that can kill the body and have power over us in this society.

“But rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.” That is the Lord. We need to fear the Lord, the one who can kill body and soul in hell.

Saul feared the Philistines and feared the people, and not the Lord. So, back to 1 Samuel 28:6: “when Saul enquired of the Lord, the Lord answered him not, neither by dreams, nor by Urim, nor by prophets.” The Lord was not dealing with Saul anymore. He went to the witch at Endor, the same kind he had put out of the land, and Samuel told him, “the Lord is departed from thee, and is become thine enemy.” Because he was bashful, self-willed, easily manipulated and made excuses, he lost the kingdom. Fear the Most High, not man.

Saul saw the host of the Philistines and “was afraid, and his heart greatly trembled.” What is fear? “For fear is nothing else but a betraying of the succours which reason offereth.”

A soldier broke it down: the succours go into comfort, and fear betrays that comfort. What reason offers is the lies you make up in your head. You trick yourself into being scared, because you make up things in your mind which ain’t really there.

And on top of that, fear is a lack of faith. Your faith is supposed to be in the Lord, but a lot of the time your faith is basically what you can see with your eyes. Saul looked at the host of the Philistines with his eyes and his heart trembled, instead of trusting the Lord who had made him king.

This is the commandment Saul turned around and broke: “There shall not be found among you any one that maketh his son or his daughter to pass through the fire, or that useth divination, or an observer of times, or an enchanter, or a witch, Or a charmer, or a consulter with familiar spirits.” The Lord said none of these would be found among Israel.

Saul had just rid the land of all of them: the soothsayers, the witches, the familiar spirits and the wizards. That is what the woman at En-dor throws back at him: “thou knowest what Saul hath done, how he hath cut off those that have familiar spirits, and the wizards, out of the land: wherefore then layest thou a snare for my life, to cause me to die?” You trying to get me killed.

Now the Lord has stopped answering him, “neither by dreams, nor by Urim, nor by prophets”, and the same man who cut them off says, “Seek me a woman that hath a familiar spirit, that I may go to her, and enquire of her.” Find me a wizard so I can know what is going on. His mind is all over the place. He is double-minded, breaking the very commandment he had enforced, and he disguises himself and goes by night so no one will see it.

That is where bashfulness leads: self-willed, disobedient, deceitful, making excuses, easily manipulated. Samuel tells him the Lord “is departed from thee, and is become thine enemy.” The Lord rent the kingdom out of his hand and gave it to David, and Saul and his sons would be with Samuel the next day. “There is that destroyeth his own soul through bashfulness.” Saul never believed in himself, so he never believed God; he had Samuel's counsel the whole time and would not listen, and when that guidance was gone he ran to the very thing the law forbade.

This is where the breaking of “the pride of your power” leads. “And upon them that are left alive of you I will send a faintness into their hearts in the lands of their enemies”. Into their minds: mentally and spiritually, you are going to be broken down. Then “the sound of a shaken leaf shall chase them”: no courage. And “they shall flee, as fleeing from a sword; and they shall fall when none pursueth.”

“And they shall fall one upon another, as it were before a sword, when none pursueth: and ye shall have no power to stand before your enemies.” Think about that spiritually. Take 2026. When black people get mad at other black people, do we show each other mercy, or do we go full-fledged? We even came up with terms for it: turning up, going savage, crashing out. But do we have that same level of aggression toward white police, or the other nations, or the Chinese? Not at all. We will stand and be aggressive with each other all day long, cuss each other out, beat each other up, kill each other. But we will not stand before the other nations. And to be clear, we do not advocate violence on anybody. The point is that the spirit is not the same toward the nations as it is toward each other.

That faintness is on the face of the African brother who said the colonizers left too early, that we are not prepared to rule ourselves. Not only defeated but subdued: low self-esteem, lack of confidence, self-hate, no faith in his own people. It is seen in a whole country left to itself that looks to the white man, to foreign aid and loans, to save it: a mall built under Chinese direction with not a brick out of place, while what our people build for ourselves has uneven steps and lopsided houses. You can’t do nothing right for yourself. That is what comes of low self-esteem.

So this is the fruit of verse 17, “they that hate you shall reign over you; and ye shall flee when none pursueth you”, and of verse 19, the pride of our power broken. These are the minds the Lord is going to use our brothers to change.
