“And thy life shall hang in doubt before thee”: in chattel slavery our lives were in doubt every day. Every day there was a chance we would be killed, a chance we might get lynched. And not only the lives of the mothers and fathers were in doubt; our sons were in doubt too. That is why verse 32 is read here: “Thy sons and thy daughters shall be given unto another people.”

That could have happened at any moment, any day. Your son ripped out of your arms to be sold to Master so-and-so, and you would never see your children again. From the day that child was born until the day someone said, I want that one as a slave, the parents lived with it, and they had nothing to say about it. “and thine eyes shall look, and fail with longing for them all the day long”: they watched their sons get taken away and watched their daughters get taken away. That is the failing of eyes and the sorrow of mind of verse 65: no way to change your reality, no future you can see for your children.

“and there shall be no might in thine hand”: no might in our hands to stop it. And there was no alcohol for them. A bottle of whiskey would not have stopped that. They had to endure this thing sober, knowing the Lord was still going to be with us somehow, some way. So they could not off themselves, because a generation was going to come from them, from the wife and from the husband, and our seed would continue while they went through trauma after trauma.

It took faith to make it from morning to night and night to morning, and they did not even have the truth the way we know it today. They pushed through all that evil and ugliness so that you and I could sit here today. So what excuse do we have? We cannot leave our post to drink and get high, or put our head inside a bottle and a crack pipe, when our forefathers endured this and kept pushing.
blog/2026/2026-05-23-2026-05-23-70-times:
Naaman was told, “Wash, and be clean”, and when he believed and obeyed the word of the prophet, he was clean. Isaiah shows what the true washing is: “Wash you, make you clean; put away the evil of your doings from before mine eyes; cease to do evil; Learn to do well”.

Put away the evil of your doings: that's the true washing. Cease to do evil, learn to do well. Action, action, action. Not speak well, do well. “seek judgment, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow.”

“though your sins be as scarlet”, bloodshot red, “they shall be as white as snow”, if you learn to do well. “though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool.” But it hangs on obedience: “If ye be willing and obedient, ye shall eat the good of the land: But if ye refuse and rebel, ye shall be devoured with the sword”.

That is Naaman. At first he refused and went away in a rage. When he humbled himself and did according to the saying of the man of God, his flesh came again like the flesh of a little child. His belief and his obedience are what made him clean.

We read about Naaman going down into the river Jordan to be cleansed. Luke brings us back to that same river: John “came into all the country about Jordan, preaching the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins; As it is written in the book of the words of Esaias the prophet, saying, The voice of one crying in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make his paths straight.”

The baptism of repentance, for the remission of sins, preached about Jordan. Naaman was washed of his leprosy in the Jordan, and John preached the washing away of sins in the same Jordan. Nothing is accidental with the Most High.

It was Christ who healed Naaman, working through Elisha by his spirit. And John in the Jordan was preparing the way of that same Lord.

Christ himself reached back and referenced this exact history. “I tell you of a truth, many widows were in Israel in the days of Elias, when the heaven was shut up three years and six months, when great famine was throughout all the land; But unto none of them was Elias sent, save unto Sarepta, a city of Sidon, unto a woman that was a widow.”

Then the point: “And many lepers were in Israel in the time of Eliseus the prophet; and none of them was cleansed, saving Naaman the Syrian.” Of all the lepers, the one cleansed was the one who humbled himself, believed, and went down and dipped seven times according to the saying of the man of God.

And seven also represents complete deliverance. Naaman dipped seven times and was delivered from his leprosy; Christ, the one whose spirit healed him through Elisha, spoke of it himself.

“Then cometh Jesus from Galilee to Jordan unto John, to be baptized of him.” Christ went unto John the Baptist to be baptized, and in what river? Jordan: the same river that Naaman had to dip in seven times.

Seven represents completion. Naaman dipped seven times in Jordan, completion in the river Jordan, and his flesh came again like the flesh of a little child. The number and the river both point to the same Christ.

Who did the healing for Naaman? Not Elisha on his own. Elisha was working by the spirit of Christ; Christ is the one who did the healing, and he used Elisha as the prophet. So when Christ himself comes to the Jordan, it is the same one who cleansed Naaman there, the one who makes us clean.

Naaman believed that the word of the prophet would heal him if he followed the commandment, going down to the river Jordan and dipping seven times. That belief is what healed him of his leprosy.

David prays the same way: “Behold, thou desirest truth in the inward parts: and in the hidden part thou shalt make me to know wisdom.” Truth in the inward parts is what the Most High desires. Then: “Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean: wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow.”

The water of the Jordan did not do it by itself; the Jordan was muddy water, and Naaman would rather have had the rivers of Damascus. The word of God is what really cleanses us of our sins. Naaman obeyed the word, and he was made clean, his flesh like the flesh of a little child.

Christ told Peter to forgive seventy times seven, and Christ never put numbers out just to put them there. Seven represents completion, but what is seventy times seven? Daniel shows it: “Seventy weeks are determined upon thy people and upon thy holy city”. That is 490 years, from Persia to Christ, “to finish the transgression, and to make an end of sins, and to make reconciliation for iniquity, and to bring in everlasting righteousness, and to seal up the vision and prophecy, and to anoint the most Holy.”

Who is the most Holy that is anointed? Hebrews 1:9 explains it: “Thou hast loved righteousness, and hated iniquity; therefore God, even thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows.” That is talking about Christ. Where Daniel says “to anoint the most Holy”, that is Christ.

So the seventy weeks run “unto the Messiah the Prince”, which is Jesus Christ, and the reconciliation for iniquity and the end of sins come through him. The prophecy was 490 years, completing that perfection through Christ, because we needed that mercy. We couldn't sacrifice when we were enslaved under Babylon and Persia; we were always in captivity, going from one captivity to the next, so we needed Christ.

The apostles said it: “Him hath God exalted with his right hand to be a Prince and a Saviour, for to give repentance to Israel”. That is why he told Peter to forgive his brother seventy times seven: because he forgave us seventy times seven. He is that complete perfection. But don't take him for granted.

“And after threescore and two weeks shall Messiah be cut off, but not for himself”: cut off for the children of Israel. “and the people of the prince that shall come shall destroy the city and the sanctuary”. That prince that shall come and destroy the sanctuary is Titus. “and the end thereof shall be with a flood, and unto the end of the war desolations are determined.” The flood is 70 AD, the destruction, and us being led away into captivity.

Christ spoke of that same desolation: “And when ye shall see Jerusalem compassed with armies, then know that the desolation thereof is nigh.” What armies? The Roman armies. That is what Daniel 9:26 is speaking of, the prince that shall come and destroy the city and the sanctuary.

Then Daniel 9:27: “in the midst of the week he shall cause the sacrifice and the oblation to cease”: the temple being destroyed. “and for the overspreading of abominations he shall make it desolate, even until the consummation”. The Roman armies around Jerusalem were the sign that the desolation determined in the seventy weeks was at hand.

So the 490 years end with Christ cut off for us and the desolation of the city by Titus. After that there was no sacrifice for us but Christ, and that is why his sacrifice is our only way through to perfection.

At the bush God told Moses, “Draw not nigh hither: put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground.” The Most High expects humility, that we humble ourselves before him. Moses was a great man in Egypt, second to Pharaoh, raised in all the customs of Egypt, and God said, I don't want to hear all of that. The shoes were symbolic.

Ecclesiastes 5:1 is what the Most High requires: “Keep thy foot when thou goest to the house of God, and be more ready to hear, than to give the sacrifice of fools: for they consider not that they do evil.” A lot of times we come with pride and contention, acting like we know. You don't know a damn thing, because if you did, you would not have followed white Jesus.

Our brothers and sisters in the world do not consider that they are in evil, and a lot of times when they come into the sanctuaries it is the same thing: pride, contention, thinking they know much when they do not. Keep thy foot means keep your mouth shut when you enter the house of God and be ready to hear, the same thing he told Moses.

The same is required of us coming into this truth. All the Christian garbage we learned, leave it outside. Islam, garbage, leave it outside. Nuwaubianism, Afrocentric, black power: all garbage. We must reform our minds as Israelites and meditate in these scriptures.

Moses asked what name to give the children of Israel, and “God said unto Moses, I AM THAT I AM: and he said, Thus shalt thou say unto the children of Israel, I AM hath sent me unto you.” So who was speaking to Moses out of the bush? You should already know: Christ.

John 8:58 proves it: “Jesus said unto them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Before Abraham was, I am.” Before Abraham was, I am. The same I AM who sent Moses to Pharaoh is Christ, speaking before Abraham ever lived. It was Christ who spoke directly to Moses.

That is why Moses could teach the gospel in the wilderness. Christ held him up on the mountain for a long season, forty days and forty nights, and showed him the secrets of the times, the beginning, the middle and the end. The God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob who came down to deliver us out of Egypt is the anointed.

Christ spoke to Abram, before his name was changed to Abraham: “Know of a surety that thy seed shall be a stranger in a land that is not theirs, and shall serve them; and they shall afflict them four hundred years.” That seed runs through Isaac, not through Abraham’s other children; Paul expounds that in Romans 9. The other nations are not God’s chosen people. And this first affliction is not America; it is ancient Egypt, where Jacob and the souls with him walked in.

So why did God bring that judgment on us? What did the sons of God do? They mixed with the daughters of men. Genesis 6: “the sons of God saw the daughters of men that they were fair; and they took them wives of all which they chose.” The sons of God are the chosen line that came out of Seth, who replaced Abel after Cain killed him.

“There were giants in the earth in those days; and also after that, when the sons of God came in unto the daughters of men, and they bare children to them, the same became mighty men which were of old, men of renown.” Then: “God saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually.” The wickedness of verse 5 is that very thing: the sons of God taking the daughters of men to themselves, when the Most High had said not to do it.

“And it repented the Lord that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him at his heart.” Now we know why the Most High told Abraham that his seed would surely end up serving in Egypt four hundred years. As the sons of God we broke his laws, and he brought forth judgment, rightfully so.

Genesis 6 says “the sons of God saw the daughters of men,” and the question always comes: who are the sons of God, and what line do they come out of? Luke 3:38 answers it at the end of Christ’s genealogy: “Which was the son of Enos, which was the son of Seth, which was the son of Adam, which was the son of God.”

That is the lineage of the sons of God. Adam is called the son of God, and the chosen line runs from him through Seth. Of Adam’s sons, Abel was put to death, and Seth replaced him; the sons of God came out of Seth’s line, down to Enos and on to Noah, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

Write that down so the next time the question comes up you are not confused. It explains the promise to Abram: “thy seed shall be a stranger in a land that is not theirs.” The sons of God of Seth’s line broke God’s law by mixing with the daughters of men, and the judgment came down on the same chosen line: Jacob’s children went into Egypt and served in hard bondage four hundred years.

Keeping the seventh day holy means more than not going to the job. Exodus 16:23 shows how the food is handled: “To morrow is the rest of the holy sabbath unto the Lord: bake that which ye will bake to day, and seethe that ye will seethe; and that which remaineth over lay up for you to be kept until the morning.”

So before Friday sundown, before complete darkness, you are to lay up your food for the next day, because there is no cooking on the Sabbath. Whatever needs baking or boiling is done the day before, and what is left over is kept for the holy day.

This is one of the laws that apply to the Sabbath, and it follows from Genesis 2:2-3: God “rested on the seventh day from all his work,” and he “blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it.” His people rest the same way, preparing ahead so that the seventh day stays free of labour.

“And on the seventh day God ended his work which he had made; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had made.” The seventh day is not Sunday. And the number seven represents completion, perfection; hold on to that, because it runs through everything that follows.

For those who are new, the Sabbath has rules. Is coming together to congregate enough? No. There are laws that apply to the Sabbath day, and the first is the commandment itself: “Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy. Six days shalt thou labour, and do all thy work: But the seventh day is the sabbath of the Lord thy God: in it thou shalt not do any work.”

So there is no working, no servile work, on the Sabbath. The commandment reaches the whole house: “thou, nor thy son, nor thy daughter, thy manservant, nor thy maidservant, nor thy cattle, nor thy stranger that is within thy gates.”

The pattern is the one God set in Genesis 2: six days of work, and on the seventh he rested. God “blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it: because that in it he had rested from all his work.” We keep it holy because he made it holy, and our rest from servile work on that day is a similitude of the true rest still to come, when we reign with Christ.

Many brothers coming out of the different religions think the Sabbath is for everyone. Exodus 31 shows who it was given to, and how seriously the Most High takes it: “Ye shall keep the sabbath therefore; for it is holy unto you: every one that defileth it shall surely be put to death: for whosoever doeth any work therein, that soul shall be cut off from among his people.”

It is “holy unto you,” to Israel. And the penalty written for defiling it, death and being cut off from among his people, shows how much weight God puts on it. It is not a day to congregate and then go about our own business; doing any work on it was a matter of life and death.

That weight comes from Genesis 2:3: “God blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it.” What God sanctifies, his people are not to make common.

Who is the Sabbath for? Exodus 31:16-17: “Wherefore the children of Israel shall keep the sabbath, to observe the sabbath throughout their generations, for a perpetual covenant. It is a sign between me and the children of Israel for ever.” Not between God and the Ammonites, not between God and the white man: the children of Israel only. When Christ comes back, yes, everyone will be made to keep the Sabbath; but the Sabbath was created for one people, the Israelites.

The reason given ties it straight to Genesis 2: “for in six days the Lord made heaven and earth, and on the seventh day he rested, and was refreshed.” The same seventh day of Genesis 2:2 is the sign of the covenant.

And it points ahead. Paul writes, “For he spake in a certain place of the seventh day on this wise, And God did rest the seventh day from all his works,” and “There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God.” The rest in the land under Joshua was not the true rest; there were enemies on every side. Resting from servile work on the seventh day is a similitude of the true rest: when Christ comes back and we reign with him a thousand years. That is why seven means completion, perfection.

Another law of the Sabbath: “Ye shall kindle no fire throughout your habitations upon the sabbath day.”

That is not talking about turning on the heat when it is freezing in the house. It is talking about cooking: do not kindle a fire to cook on the Sabbath. It goes together with Exodus 16:23, where the food is baked and boiled the day before and laid up until the morning.

And stop following Amalek, the so-called Jewish people who are not the real Jews, who add to the law with their Talmud, their oral law. Their additions make the Sabbath a burden God never put on it. The commandment is what is written: no cooking fire in our habitations on the day God blessed and sanctified, the seventh day on which he “rested from all his work which God created and made.”

Lamech’s “seventy and sevenfold” was complete vengeance, and Edom carries that same spirit. Amos 1:11: “Thus saith the Lord; For three transgressions of Edom, and for four, I will not turn away the punishment thereof; because he did pursue his brother with the sword, and did cast off all pity, and his anger did tear perpetually, and he kept his wrath for ever.”

He pursued his brother Jacob with the sword. He cast off all pity. His anger tore perpetually, and “he kept his wrath for ever.” Forever, perpetual: he hates our guts, and it does not wear off with time.

That is why we cannot trust this man, and why people wonder to this day why they still treat us the way they do. He has not forgotten how we ruled over him, and he is still acting out his vengeance. The Lord has seen it, and he says he will not turn away the punishment for it.

This is the dark side of seventy times seven. On the one side is the murderer’s total vengeance, kept forever; on the other side, as the class went on to show, is Christ answering Peter, “I say not unto thee, Until seven times: but, Until seventy times seven”: complete, boundless mercy for Israel.

God said of Cain, “whosoever slayeth Cain, vengeance shall be taken on him sevenfold.” Then Cain’s great-great-grandson Lamech boasted to his wives, Adah and Zillah: “I have slain a man to my wounding, and a young man to my hurt. If Cain shall be avenged sevenfold, truly Lamech seventy and sevenfold.” He walked in the same footsteps as Cain; through regeneration it would be no surprise if Lamech were Cain all over again. Seventy and sevenfold in the mouth of a murderer means complete vengeance: total and utter.

That is why Ecclesiasticus says never trust thine enemy. You think he forgot how we handled him under King David, when we put garrisons over him and pushed him off the mountains? Or that we pushed him into the wilderness, where they became the wildlings of the dark ages? He has not forgotten. He is still acting out his vengeance on the so-called blacks and Hispanics to this day.

Ezekiel 35:5 names it: “Because thou hast had a perpetual hatred, and hast shed the blood of the children of Israel by the force of the sword in the time of their calamity, in the time that their iniquity had an end.” Perpetual hatred is great hatred, ongoing hatred, fiery hatred. That is Lamech’s seventy and sevenfold carried on through Edom.

The death of Patrice Lumumba shows it. One of the officers responsible spoke on video, laughing, this damn devil: they chopped up his body and poured acid on it, and he kept Lumumba’s gold tooth. His family held it until it was recently flown back to the Congo. The same was done to Nat Turner, whose skull was passed down as an heirloom, a trophy. These people are the damn devil the Bible speaks of, and that is the perpetual hatred.

Edom’s hatred is perpetual, like Lamech’s vengeance, “seventy and sevenfold,” complete and total. But God has spoken on what will come of it. Obadiah 1:10: “For thy violence against thy brother Jacob shame shall cover thee, and thou shalt be cut off for ever.”

For his violence against his brother Jacob, shame shall cover him, and he shall be cut off forever. His wrath is kept forever, and his end is forever too.

So Lamech’s seventy and seven was complete vengeance, driven by hatred, perpetual hatred. Then comes the flip side. Peter asked, “Lord, how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? till seven times?” and “Jesus saith unto him, I say not unto thee, Until seven times: but, Until seventy times seven.” Christ took the same number and made it complete mercy. He forgave us through all our captivities, and he commands us to forgive our brother the same way, while the enemy who kept his wrath for ever is cut off for ever.

Isaiah calls us “a people laden with iniquity.” Christ answers that very word: “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” Heavy laden with what? With sin, the iniquity Isaiah just named.

That is why we are in need of a saviour. We read the history of our forefathers in the wilderness: the Most High showed great signs and wonders, and we were still a stiff-necked, hard-headed people. We are “a sinful nation”, “a seed of evildoers, children that are corrupters.” We forsake the Lord every time we sin, and we have “provoked the Holy One of Israel unto anger.” That is why the so-called blacks and Hispanics went into captivity, just as Deuteronomy 28:15 through 68 laid out the curses for breaking the commandments. Many of our brothers and sisters are still going backward, moonwalking away from the Most High. Brothers and sisters, we cannot do it without Christ.

So be honest and sincere, even in prayer. Do not go to the Most High acting righteous when you are full of dead bones, sin and guile. None of us is righteous; we are trying, but there is sin still in us. Open your mouth and confess the things you are battling with.

“and I will give you rest.” That rest is not a good night’s sleep. It is our land, the kingdom of God, rulership for a thousand years under Christ. That is the true rest he is talking about, but we have to come unto him. Now is our time to get our minds right and repent.

At Jericho it was sevens all the way through: “seven priests shall bear before the ark seven trumpets of rams’ horns: and the seventh day ye shall compass the city seven times, and the priests shall blow with the trumpets.” Six days they went round once, and on the seventh day, the Sabbath day, seven times. “And it came to pass at the seventh time, when the priests blew with the trumpets, Joshua said unto the people, Shout; for the Lord hath given you the city.” Because of their faith, on the seventh day the Most High brought the walls down flat.

Revelation shows the same pattern at the end: “And the seventh angel sounded; and there were great voices in heaven, saying, The kingdoms of this world are become the kingdoms of our Lord, and of his Christ; and he shall reign for ever and ever.” The seventh angel sounded the trump, and that brought forth completion. It is the same thing that happened when our forefathers walked around the walls of Jericho.

Seven represents completion and totality, and it also represents complete deliverance. Nothing is accidental with the Most High; he uses seven as a form of deliverance. From the beginning it has been there: the seventh day rest, Naaman dipped seven times, and Jericho compassed seven times by seven priests with seven trumpets.

So the seventh trumpet at Jericho gave Israel the city, and the seventh trumpet in Revelation gives the kingdoms of this world to our Lord and his Christ. All of this is a representation of Christ, and it points to the complete deliverance of Israel when he reigns.

“Purge out therefore the old leaven, that ye may be a new lump, as ye are unleavened. For even Christ our passover is sacrificed for us”.

The old leaven is sin. Purge it out, that you may be a new lump. Because Christ our passover is sacrificed for us.

Christ was that unleavened bread that laid his life down for the children of Israel. So the passover and the feast of unleavened bread in Leviticus 23:5-6 both come to him: he is the lamb and he is the bread. With these the class counted three of the seven so far: the Sabbath, the passover, and the feast of unleavened bread.

Peter shows who that lamb without blemish was: “ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold, from your vain conversation received by tradition from your fathers; But with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot”.

So Christ was that lamb without blemish, the same thing Exodus 12:5 required. Without blemish and without spot. He is the one “foreordained before the foundation of the world, but was manifest in these last times for you”.

That is what John the Baptist said of Christ when he saw him coming: Behold the Lamb of God that takes away the sins of the world. The passover of Leviticus 23:5 is fulfilled in him.

Still in the passover instructions: “In one house shall it be eaten; thou shalt not carry forth ought of the flesh abroad out of the house; neither shall ye break a bone thereof.”

Neither shall ye break a bone thereof. Those are the instructions for how to slaughter the lamb: do not break the bones of it.

That one command is going to be fulfilled to the letter in Christ. The high holy day of passover that we just went over is a picture of him, down to his bones.

Leviticus 23 lays out the feasts of the Lord, seven of them in that chapter, and every single one of them represents Jesus Christ. The first annual one is the Lord’s passover, “In the fourteenth day of the first month at even”, the high holy day we just celebrated. So we go back to the instructions for the passover lamb.

“Your lamb shall be without blemish, a male of the first year: ye shall take it out from the sheep, or from the goats”. Without blemish, a male of the first year. That is the lamb our forefathers had to choose.

That lamb without blemish is the pattern of Christ. The passover is a representation of Christ laying down his life for us, and everything spoken of the lamb in Exodus 12 points to him.

This is the fulfilment. “The Jews therefore, because it was the preparation, that the bodies should not remain upon the cross on the sabbath day, (for that sabbath day was an high day,) besought Pilate that their legs might be broken”.

“Then came the soldiers, and brake the legs of the first, and of the other which was crucified with him. But when they came to Jesus, and saw that he was dead already, they brake not his legs”.

They broke the legs of the two crucified with him, but not his. Thus fulfilling the prophecy in Psalms 34:20, and the passover command, neither shall ye break a bone thereof. Christ was that passover lamb, and there is still more meat to scrape off the bones of this.

After passover comes the next feast: “on the fifteenth day of the same month is the feast of unleavened bread unto the Lord: seven days ye must eat unleavened bread.” There is that seven again.

The unleavened bread represents Christ: his sinless life, not having leaven. We know the history too, the Most High wanted us to hurry up and leave Egypt, so there was no time to sit and bake bread. But it also goes into Christ’s unleavened life, sinless and blameless.

Christ says it: “I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger”. He is the bread of life, the unleavened bread of the feast.

“And Joseph also went up from Galilee, out of the city of Nazareth, into Judea, unto the city of David, which is called Bethlehem; (because he was of the house and lineage of David:) To be taxed with Mary his espoused wife, being great with child.”

To be taxed together you have to be married, brothers. You have to have papers, jointly. Not a toilet paper: years ago a brother wrote an instrument of divorce on toilet paper, because he did not really value her or count her as his wife.

“And so it was, that, while they were there, the days were accomplished that she should be delivered. And she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes”. They wrapped Christ in swaddling clothes, the same thing our forefathers did with the lambs when they brought them to Jerusalem.

Born in Bethlehem where the passover lambs were raised, wrapped the way they were wrapped, offered in Jerusalem at passover. Thus fulfilling prophecy. So we know Christ was our passover.

The lambs without blemish were raised in Bethlehem and slaughtered in Jerusalem. Same thing as Jesus Christ. So the prophecy: “But thou, Beth–lehem Ephratah, though thou be little among the thousands of Judah, yet out of thee shall he come forth unto me that is to be ruler in Israel; whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting.”

Christ was born in Bethlehem. An article read in the class shows how our forefathers handled the passover lambs: the high priests given charge over them brought forth lambs without blemish from Migdal Eder in Bethlehem, wrapped in cloths, and brought them to Jerusalem for sacrifice. Migdal Eder means the tower of the flock, the same tower of the flock read about in Micah the fourth chapter, the eighth verse.

This Jesus was born in Bethlehem, wrapped in cloths, and eventually brought to Jerusalem during passover, where he offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins. The same road as the lambs.

Here is the prophecy about Christ: “He keepeth all his bones: not one of them is broken.”

What was commanded for the passover lamb in Exodus 12:46, “neither shall ye break a bone thereof”, is written here as a prophecy of the Messiah. Not one of his bones would be broken.

The passover is a representation of Christ laying down his life for us, and the Psalms spoke it ahead of time, so that when it came to pass we would know he is our passover.

The two wave loaves of Leviticus 23:17 “are the firstfruits unto the Lord.” Paul shows who the firstfruits are: “But now is Christ risen from the dead, and become the firstfruits of them that slept.” Christ is the firstfruits.

“For since by man came death, by man came also the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive.” Then the order is set: “But every man in his own order: Christ the firstfruits; afterward they that are Christ’s at his coming.”

The same promise stands for us if we believe and keep the commandments in the faith of Christ: first Christ was raised, and afterward we that are his are raised at his coming.

Like the sabbath, the passover and the feast of unleavened bread before it, the feast of firstfruits is a representation of Christ. All seven of the high holy days read in Leviticus 23 represent Jesus Christ, and seven sabbaths counted “complete” to the fifty days points to completion in him.

James says it the same way: “Of his own will begat he us with the word of truth, that we should be a kind of firstfruits of his creatures.”

The Most High, of his own will, begat us with the word of truth for this purpose, that we should be a kind of firstfruits. We become that if we follow after Christ’s example, since Christ is the firstfruits risen from the dead.

So the feast of firstfruits in Leviticus 23:15-17, the new offering brought to the Lord after seven sabbaths complete, is a picture of Christ and of the people he begets by the word: the best of the best, offered unto the Lord.

Revelation shows the firstfruits standing with Christ: “These are they which were not defiled with women; for they are virgins.” Not defiled with philosophy, not defiled with false doctrine, and also not defiled with a literal woman.

“These are they which follow the Lamb whithersoever he goeth. These were redeemed from among men, being the firstfruits unto God and to the Lamb.” They follow Christ wherever he goes, and they are redeemed from among men.

This is the end of the feast of firstfruits in Leviticus 23: Christ the firstfruits risen, and afterward those that are his, kept clean from the world’s doctrine and its filth, offered as “the firstfruits unto the Lord.”

Christ is the firstfruits, and his people are called firstfruits with him: “And not only they, but ourselves also, which have the firstfruits of the Spirit, even we ourselves groan within ourselves, waiting for the adoption, to wit, the redemption of our body.”

Redemption of what body? The body that we used to have, when we were in the heavens with Christ. That is what we groan and wait for.

We are supposed to be the firstfruits: the crème de la crème, the best of the best, if we would repent in Christ. So the “firstfruits unto the Lord” brought out of Israel’s habitations in Leviticus 23:17 point not only to Christ risen, but to the Israelites who have his Spirit and wait for their redemption.

The trumpet sound at Christ’s coming is no flute and no harmonica. Ezra says: “And the trumpet shall give a sound, which when every man heareth, they shall be suddenly afraid.”

That is how you know it is not talking about a soft sound or any instrument you could think of. Every man who hears it is suddenly afraid. That trumpet is a frightening sound.

It lines up with Matthew 24:31, the “great sound of a trumpet” that gathers the elect, and with Zechariah 9:14, where “the Lord God shall blow the trumpet” and his arrow goes forth as the lightning. The feast of trumpets in Leviticus 23:24-25 is a memorial pointing to that day: the gathering of Israel, and terror for the nations.

Why do we blow the trumpet? Because it was commanded of us, on the new moons and on our high holy days: “a memorial of blowing of trumpets, an holy convocation.” But like every one of these feasts, it is a representation of Christ.

Christ says: “And he shall send his angels with a great sound of a trumpet, and they shall gather together his elect from the four winds, from one end of heaven to the other.” The trumpet sounds at his coming, and it gathers his elect.

The elect is only Israel, not all nations. They are gathered “from one end of heaven to the other” because we were scattered from one end of heaven to the other. That tells you who the children of God are: the only people scattered from one end of the earth to the other are the so-called blacks and Hispanics, the Israelites.

So the feast of trumpets looks forward to that great sound, when Christ sends his angels to gather his scattered people home.

That trumpet is not talking about a flute or some soft sound. When Christ comes back, everybody is going to fear. Zechariah shows it: “And the Lord shall be seen over them, and his arrow shall go forth as the lightning: and the Lord God shall blow the trumpet, and shall go with whirlwinds of the south.” This is when we are going to conquer the nations.

“The Lord of hosts shall defend them; and they shall devour, and subdue with sling stones”. We are going to devour all these nations, put them under our feet, break them in half. Then “they shall drink, and make a noise as through wine; and they shall be filled like bowls, and as the corners of the altar.”

“And the Lord their God shall save them in that day as the flock of his people: for they shall be as the stones of a crown, lifted up as an ensign upon his land.” The Most High said he is going to save us. That is some beautiful stuff right there.

So the memorial of blowing of trumpets in Leviticus 23:24 points to the day the Lord God himself blows the trumpet, defends Israel, and lifts his people up like the stones of a crown upon his land.

John says it plainly: “And he is the propitiation for our sins”. Christ is the atonement for our sins, the fulfilment of the day of atonement in Leviticus 23:27.

Then: “and not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world.” That world is the scattered Israelites, all Israel, so that they may have time to repent. It is talking about Israel; it is not talking about all nations.

The next reading shows it: in the high priest’s long garment “was the whole world”, and that world was the twelve tribes. So when Christ atones for the world, he atones for Israel wherever they have been scattered.

The day of atonement, when Israel was to “afflict your souls, and offer an offering made by fire unto the Lord”, is a representation of Christ. Christ was that atonement.

“By so much was Jesus made a surety of a better testament.” The better testament is the new covenant. “And they truly were many priests, because they were not suffered to continue by reason of death”: the priests under the law died, one after another.

“But this man, because he continueth ever, hath an unchangeable priesthood. Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him”. Christ is the true high priest, with no death in him. That is how he is able to atone for our sins continually, where the old priests could only atone until they died.

“But Christ being come an high priest of good things to come, by a greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made with hands, that is to say, not of this building; Neither by the blood of goats and calves, but by his own blood he entered in once into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption for us.” His blood was given for atonement, and he died only once. Eternal redemption for whom? For us, the Israelites.

“For if the blood of bulls and of goats, and the ashes of an heifer sprinkling the unclean, sanctifieth to the purifying of the flesh: How much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without spot to God, purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God?” Without spot means blameless: he had no sin.

“And for this cause he is the mediator of the new testament”, just as Moses was the mediator for us when we came up out of Egypt, so “that by means of death, for the redemption of the transgressions that were under the first testament, they which are called might receive the promise of eternal inheritance.” That promise is ours if we believe.

“For where a testament is, there must also of necessity be the death of the testator.” For the testament to come to fruition and be valid, the testator had to die. That is why Christ had to die. “For a testament is of force after men are dead: otherwise it is of no strength at all while the testator liveth.” While a man is alive, his testament can still change. “Whereupon neither the first testament was dedicated without blood.” Blood had to be spilled for the first covenant of animal sacrifice too. The yearly atonement of Leviticus 23:27 was fulfilled once for all in Christ’s own blood.

Paul names what Christ is: “Whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation through faith in his blood”. God sent Christ forth, and propitiation means atonement.

He was set forth “to declare his righteousness for the remission of sins that are past, through the forbearance of God”. The sins that are past are forgiven through faith in his blood, by God’s forbearance toward us.

So the day of atonement, when Israel afflicted their souls and brought an offering by fire, finds its meaning in Christ. He is the atonement God himself set forth, and we receive it through faith in his blood.

Remember, Christ is the new high priest. Wisdom shows what the high priest carried: “For in the long garment was the whole world, and in the four rows of the stones was the glory of the fathers graven, and thy Majesty upon the diadem of his head.”

That is Aaron the high priest, and the long garment is the ephod. There was a stone for each tribe. The whole world on Aaron’s chest was Israel. It did not represent the Moabites, the Ammonites, the Hittites, the Perizzites or the Ishmaelites; only the Israelites.

That is how 1 John 2:2 is understood: Christ is “the propitiation for our sins: and not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world.” The world the high priest bore before God on the day of atonement was the twelve tribes, and the world Christ atones for as the new high priest is scattered Israel.

“The fifteenth day of this seventh month shall be the feast of tabernacles for seven days unto the Lord.” Another word for tabernacles is sukkot, booths, and it means to dwell.

John shows who the feast points to: “And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,)”. The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us: he pitched his tent among us. Christ walked among us.

So the feast of tabernacles, like the sabbath, the passover, unleavened bread, firstfruits, trumpets and atonement before it, is a representation of Christ. The seven days of dwelling in booths look to the Son of God coming to dwell with his people in the flesh.

“Jesus answered and said unto them, Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” The Jews took him simply: “Forty and six years was this temple in building, and wilt thou rear it up in three days?” They thought he meant the building.

“But he spake of the temple of his body.” His body is the temple, the tabernacle. Hebrews 9:11 shows it: “But Christ being come an high priest of good things to come, by a greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made with hands, that is to say, not of this building”. His body was that greater and more perfect tabernacle. “Neither by the blood of goats and calves, but by his own blood he entered in once into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption for us.”

So the booths Israel dwelt in for the feast of tabernacles point to Christ’s own body, the true tabernacle in which God dwelt among us, destroyed and raised up again in three days.

“And I heard a great voice out of heaven saying, Behold, the tabernacle of God is with men, and he will dwell with them”. That is what tabernacle means: to dwell. He shall dwell with whom? The Israelites.

Then: “and they shall be his people, and God himself shall be with them, and be their God.” All praises to the Most High for that. He is not the God of the Ishmaelites, not the God of the Arabs, not the God of the white man. He is the God of Israel only.

This is the completion every feast was pointing to. All seven of the high holy days read in Leviticus 23, and there are more, represent Jesus Christ, and the feast of tabernacles ends where the scriptures end: God dwelling with his people Israel for ever.

“Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness”, the mercy Christ offers us, “humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering”: longsuffering toward the brother who repents. “Forbearing one another”, as Christ forbears us, “and forgiving one another”.

Forgiving is something some of us need to pray for. Some can forgive nothing and hold on to grudges like there is no tomorrow. Imagine if Christ held on to grudges against us. We would not be here; we would be in hell with white Jesus, Islam and our sins. The only reason we are here is Jesus Christ and his boundless mercy toward us.

“If any man have a quarrel against any: even as Christ forgave you, so also do ye.” Christ does not put numbers out just to put them. Seventy times seven is 490, and Daniel's seventy weeks, 490 years from Persia to Christ, were determined “to make an end of sins, and to make reconciliation for iniquity” through the Messiah cut off for the children of Israel. We could not sacrifice in Babylon and Persia; we needed Christ, the complete perfection of mercy. He forgave us seventy times seven, so we forgive our brother the same, and we do not take him for granted.

Lamech's seventy and sevenfold was complete vengeance, the perpetual hatred Esau carries against his brother Jacob. Now the flip side: Peter asked, “Lord, how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? till seven times?” Christ answered, “I say not unto thee, Until seven times: but, Until seventy times seven.” Christ offers boundless, endless mercy to the Israelites who believe, and he told Peter to do the same.

Luke gives the terms: “Take heed to yourselves: If thy brother trespass against thee, rebuke him; and if he repent, forgive him.” That brother is the children of thy people, as Leviticus 19:17 says. It is rebuke first, then repentance, then forgiveness.

“And if he trespass against thee seven times in a day, and seven times in a day turn again to thee, saying, I repent; thou shalt forgive him.” Why? Seven represents completion. The same way Christ forgave us when we were without sacrifice and without mercy: all our adulteries, fornication, lying and stealing during Assyria, Babylon, Persia and America, scattered in Africa in the dark ages doing all sorts of wicked things. Christ forgave all of that. That is why he said seventy times seven.

To expound further on Christ being the ultimate sacrifice: “Wherefore when he cometh into the world, he saith, Sacrifice and offering thou wouldest not, but a body hast thou prepared me”. The body was Christ. The sacrificial laws of animal sacrifice were a preparation for what was to come, a shadow of good things to come; the good thing that came was the body of Jesus Christ, dying only for the nation of Israel.

“In burnt offerings and sacrifices for sin thou hast had no pleasure.” The Most High had no pleasure in those sacrifices. They were temporary, to train us and prepare us for Christ.

“Then said I, Lo, I come (in the volume of the book it is written of me,) to do thy will, O God.” In the volume of the book: the whole book, not just the New Testament. Christ is present in the Old Testament, and Christ is present before the Old Testament.

“Above when he said, Sacrifice and offering and burnt offerings and offering for sin thou wouldest not, neither hadst pleasure therein; which are offered by the law”. So the offerings of the law pointed to the body prepared for him, the one sacrifice that saves his people from their sins.

We did not return to what the Most High commanded, the feasts he told us to go back to, and that is why we were in need of a saviour, an ultimate sacrifice. From Abraham to David, from David to the carrying away into Babylon, and from Babylon to Christ were fourteen generations each; we were always in slavery.

“And she shall bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins.” His name means he saves. His people: the Israelites only. From their sins. That is why he was the ultimate sacrifice.

His cousin John expounds on it: “Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world.” The Lamb of God. Christ was that perfect, ultimate sacrifice, the lamb that takes away the sins of the people he came to save.

Christ was always the plan. He is the author, the executive producer, whatever title you want to give him. From before the Old Testament, the body prepared for him in the volume of the book was the plan for saving his people from their sins.

John shows it: “All things were made by him”. All things were made by Christ: the principalities, the things you see out in space, the worlds, with an s. “And without him was not any thing made that was made.”

The one who made all things is the one who came as the Lamb of God to save his people. The sacrifices of the law, the seventh day and the rest it points to were all his from the beginning. So when the angel said “thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins”, it was the Maker of all things coming to fulfil the plan that was always his.

Numbers 14:22 says they “have tempted me now these ten times, and have not hearkened to my voice”. These ten times are the countless acts of stubbornness of the children of Israel, and that is why the Lord asked “How long will this people provoke me?” Write them down. The Most High deals in numbers, and nothing in the Bible is insignificant.

Number one is at the Red Sea. “And they said unto Moses, Because there were no graves in Egypt, hast thou taken us away to die in the wilderness? wherefore hast thou dealt thus with us, to carry us forth out of Egypt? Is not this the word that we did tell thee in Egypt, saying, Let us alone, that we may serve the Egyptians? For it had been better for us to serve the Egyptians, than that we should die in the wilderness.”

They were complaining to Moses. The Lord had just brought them out with his glory and his miracles, and the first thing they did at the sea was wish themselves back in Egypt serving the Egyptians.

Number two of the ten times the children of Israel tempted the Lord is at Marah, m-a-r-a-h. Write it down so you are not confused if it comes up again.

“And when they came to Marah, they could not drink of the waters of Marah, for they were bitter: therefore the name of it was called Marah. And the people murmured against Moses, saying, What shall we drink?”

The people complained because the water was bitter. They had just seen the Lord overthrow the Egyptians in the midst of the sea, and at the first bitter water they murmured against Moses. That is the provoking the Lord speaks of in Numbers 14:22: men “which have seen my glory, and my miracles”, and still did not hearken to his voice.

Number four is the hoarding of the manna. “And Moses said, Let no man leave of it till the morning.” Moses gave specific instructions: do not leave any of the manna until the morning.

“Notwithstanding they hearkened not unto Moses; but some of them left of it until the morning, and it bred worms, and stank: and Moses was wroth with them.” Moses just told you. And they said, the hell with you; we want to replace you anyway. That is the mindset of our people.

This is what the Lord means in Numbers 14:22 when he says they “have not hearkened to my voice.” He fed them bread from heaven, gave one plain instruction, and they would not keep it.

Number three is the wilderness of Sin. “And the whole congregation of the children of Israel murmured against Moses and Aaron in the wilderness”. Do you notice a trend here?

“Would to God we had died by the hand of the Lord in the land of Egypt, when we sat by the flesh pots, and when we did eat bread to the full; for ye have brought us forth into this wilderness, to kill this whole assembly with hunger.”

It is going to be the same thing when Christ comes back, but Christ is not playing games with us this time; he did not play games back then either. This time it will be ten times worse, ten times more severe, ten times more strict. When we are saved out of this modern day Egypt, Babylon the Great, America, the United Snakes of America, and Christ brings us into the wilderness, that grace is finished. No more I should have, could have, would have, I made a mistake. That is over with.

Number five is the Sabbath manna. “And it came to pass, that there went out some of the people on the seventh day for to gather, and they found none. And the Lord said unto Moses, How long refuse ye to keep my commandments and my laws? See, for that the Lord hath given you the sabbath, therefore he giveth you on the sixth day the bread of two days; abide ye every man in his place, let no man go out of his place on the seventh day.”

They were supposed to gather extra on the sixth day; the Most High gave them enough manna to lay up for two days. And they said, no, Lord, we are going out on the seventh day to get this manna. Forgetting everything the Most High did for us in bringing us up out of Egypt. No gratitude. We are a people of no gratitude at all.

Number six is at Massah and Meribah. “Wherefore the people did chide with Moses, and said, Give us water that we may drink.” To chide means to murmur, to be contentious, to go back and forth. “And Moses said unto them, Why chide ye with me? wherefore do ye tempt the Lord?”

Then, “the people murmured against Moses, and said, Wherefore is this that thou hast brought us up out of Egypt, to kill us and our children and our cattle with thirst? And Moses cried unto the Lord, saying, What shall I do unto this people? they be almost ready to stone me.” They were almost ready to stone the man who brought them out of Egypt, over water.

The Lord said, “Behold, I will stand before thee there upon the rock in Horeb; and thou shalt smite the rock, and there shall come water out of it, that the people may drink.” And Moses “called the name of the place Massah, and Meribah, because of the chiding of the children of Israel, and because they tempted the Lord, saying, Is the Lord among us, or not?”

That is the very word Numbers 14:22 uses: they have “tempted me now these ten times.” The place itself was named for it.

Number seven is the golden calf. “And when the people saw that Moses delayed to come down out of the mount, the people gathered themselves together unto Aaron, and said unto him, Up, make us gods, which shall go before us; for as for this Moses, the man that brought us up out of the land of Egypt, we wot not what is become of him.”

That is the no gratitude. The Most High just showed all those wonderful plagues and destroyed your enemy, and now you want a different god, a god of silver, gold and wood, a god that cannot talk. And look how disrespectful: as for this Moses. No different from our people who despise this truth and want to go back to Christianity, who prefer white Jesus, or who run to the east, to Mecca, and pray to a damn cobblestone that cannot talk back or answer prayers. That is why the Most High says we are dumber than an ox.

Aaron, the high priest, got real simple here, but it was out of fear, and he knew better. Then, “he received them at their hand, and fashioned it with a graving tool, after he had made it a molten calf”; he had the skills of a blacksmith and turned the gold they spoiled from Egypt into idolatry. It was the people who said “These be thy gods, O Israel, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt.” Then “the people sat down to eat and to drink, and rose up to play”: in honour of that pagan god they had orgies.

“They have turned aside quickly out of the way which I commanded them”. “I have seen this people, and, behold, it is a stiffnecked people: Now therefore let me alone, that my wrath may wax hot against them, and that I may consume them”. Yes, we are a stiffnecked people, and only Moses standing in the gap turned it away, as he did again in Numbers 14.

Number eight is Taberah. “And when the people complained, it displeased the Lord: and the Lord heard it; and his anger was kindled; and the fire of the Lord burnt among them, and consumed them that were in the uttermost parts of the camp.” More complaining, and the Most High started burning people with fire, the same thing he is going to do in America. “And the people cried unto Moses; and when Moses prayed unto the Lord, the fire was quenched.”

Then the lusting for flesh: “the mixt multitude that was among them fell a lusting: and the children of Israel also wept again, and said, Who shall give us flesh to eat? We remember the fish, which we did eat in Egypt freely; the cucumbers, and the melons, and the leeks, and the onions, and the garlick”. Always about food; black people for you.

“But now our soul is dried away: there is nothing at all, beside this manna, before our eyes.” Ungrateful, complaining about the manna. Over and over the Lord was longsuffering, and over and over Moses prayed and the Lord pardoned, as Numbers 14:20 says: “I have pardoned according to thy word”.

Number nine: the lusting for flesh ended in a graveyard. “And he called the name of that place Kibroth–hattaavah: because there they buried the people that lusted.” Taberah was number eight; Kibroth-hattaavah is number nine.

Number ten is the report of the spies, the doubt and fear of Numbers 13 and 14, and there the Most High had enough. “Surely they shall not see the land which I sware unto their fathers, neither shall any of them that provoked me see it”. Everyone twenty and upward fell in the wilderness, save Caleb and Joshua.

The Most High deals in numbers, and everything in the Bible is significant. Ten times he was longsuffering, and places like Kibroth-hattaavah still carry the names of what our fathers did.

Wisdom “hath hewn out her seven pillars”. Let's see who this wisdom pertains to and who had these seven pillars. Isaiah: “And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots”. That is talking about Christ.

Now count what rests upon him. “And the spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him”: that's one. “the spirit of wisdom”: two. “and understanding”: three. “the spirit of counsel”: four. “And might”: five. “the spirit of knowledge”: six. “and of the fear of the Lord”: seven.

Those are the seven pillars of wisdom that Christ had. Seven represents completion, so they represent complete spiritual perfection, and that is what Christ operated in. Wisdom's house on seven pillars is Christ, full of the spirit of the Lord in every part.

“Wisdom hath builded her house”. Who is this wisdom? Go back a chapter, where wisdom speaks: “The Lord possessed me in the beginning of his way, before his works of old. I was set up from everlasting, from the beginning, or ever the earth was.”

This is going into Christ and wisdom, one and the same, interchangeable. Christ is the ultimate wisdom, the complete wisdom, set up from everlasting before the earth was.

That is why chapter 9 says wisdom “hath hewn out her seven pillars”. Seven represents completion, and Christ is complete wisdom. The house wisdom built stands on him, the one the Lord possessed in the beginning of his way.

The question put to the class: you're alone online late at night, temptation hits, and nobody from the congregation would know. What shows integrity? A, entertain the temptation privately. B, watch a little and justify it later. C, cut it off immediately and fight temptation. D, convince yourself grace covers everything. Answer D is a scary mindset to have, and Paul already answered it: “What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound?”

Shall we continue in sin that grace may cover everything? That is a terrible mindset, and it is the mindset of Christianity: I found grace, grace covers me, I can do what I want when I want. All I have to do is believe in Jesus; I ain't got to do nothing he says, just believe he's my Lord and savior. Christianity is evil.

The answer is C. The questions are easy and the answers are easy; the problem is when it comes to fruition in real time. You are fighting your war against yourself: you don't want to push play, but you want to push play, and nobody is there to tell you a damn thing. That is when C gets blurred out.

The real battlefield is private. A lot of people fall spiritually in secret long before they fall publicly. The representative shows up at the Sabbath; the real you shows up at home, alone, with your family, and your wife knows exactly who you are. You can't salute so hard you're over righteous and then go home and verbally, financially or physically abuse your wife. And sisters, you can't bow 90 degrees at the door and then go home, cuss your husband out, and keep a filthy house. That is lacking integrity and poor character.

That is Proverbs 11:3: “The integrity of the upright shall guide them: but the perverseness of transgressors shall destroy them.” Grace is not a cover for sin; integrity is acting on what you know, even when nobody is watching.

“He that refuseth instruction despiseth his own soul”. He doesn't want to hear it; he doesn't want to be corrected; he's always right, but wrong as hell. That isn't hurting somebody else; you are destroying your own soul, because you can't be corrected, which means you can't grow. This is why: “A reproof entereth more into a wise man than an hundred stripes into a fool.”

As a foolish person, you cannot allow wisdom to enter in. You're sitting around the men, you're in the school with all these men, you see everybody growing around you, and for some reason you know everything, but the wisdom can't take hold and exalt you the way it exalts all the rest who take hold of it. You're fighting against it.

That is why some have been in the truth 10 or 15 years and are still a soldier. How long you been with us? 10 years. What's your rank? Officer of 10, sir. Why? I don't know, sir. You know. You know everything else but that. You can't say you've been held back. Ten years and you're only able to deal with ten men: that is a problem.

That is when it is time to take stock in yourself, and a lot of people don't want to do that, because they don't want the integrity that comes with the Bible. The one who hears reproof gets understanding; the fool takes a hundred stripes and learns nothing.

“the Lord was with Joseph, and he was a prosperous man.” His master saw that the Lord was with him and made him overseer over his house, and “the Lord blessed the Egyptian’s house for Joseph’s sake.” And “Joseph was a goodly person, and well favoured”: he had a very good reputation, and people looked at him as a man of integrity and good character.

Then his master’s wife “cast her eyes upon Joseph; and she said, Lie with me.” He refused: his master had committed all that he had to his hand, “neither hath he kept back any thing from me but thee, because thou art his wife: how then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?” Nobody was watching him. He could have done it, but he said no. That is where integrity comes from: making the right decision when nobody is watching.

Ecclesiasticus 9:9 gives the same wisdom as a command: “Sit not at all with another man’s wife, nor sit down with her in thine arms, and spend not thy money with her at the wine; lest thine heart incline unto her, and so through thy desire thou fall into destruction.” Do not sit with another man’s wife at all. Do not play with it. Do not be drinking around somebody else’s wife, because your heart will incline to her, and both of you will destroy everything.

Joseph lived that. When “there was none of the men of the house there within,” she caught him by his garment, “and he left his garment in her hand, and fled.” He knew it was wickedness that would destroy his reputation and everything he had worked so hard for, and that he would not only be sinning against her but against the Lord. He fled rather than sit with it, even though he went to prison when she lied on him.

Job's three friends heard of all the evil that came upon him, came every one from his own place “to mourn with him and to comfort him”, and “sat down with him upon the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spake a word unto him: for they saw that his grief was very great.” Now you see the type of men you are around. That is true friendship, and Galatians shows what it is supposed to do.

“Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted.” When a brother falls, you have to build and restore this man back to life. Speak life into that brother to get him back on track, in meekness, remembering you could be tempted too.

“Bear ye one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.” If we were in that same situation, we would want our brothers to come and get us out of it.

Job held fast his integrity when he lost his kids, lost everything he had, and had boils all over his body. Satan came in through his wife, “curse God, and die”, but Job answered, “shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?” A man going through that needs brothers who will sit with him, carry his burden with him and restore him, not tear him down.

Judas is the character we are not to have. “This he said, not that he cared for the poor; but because he was a thief, and had the bag.” He walked with Christ and saw many miracles, and still betrayed the savior and everybody around him. Money was his root and his god: greed. That is how they infiltrate organizations: they come in and offer money, and a people lacking integrity gives up the organization and lets money dictate and control the movement. That ain't happening here.

Israel is to give the nations the opposite: “Keep therefore and do them; for this is your wisdom and your understanding in the sight of the nations, which shall hear all these statutes, and say, Surely this great nation is a wise and understanding people.” Keeping the law is our wisdom, and it is seen.

When your coworkers wonder why this brother doesn't murmur with them and never works the Sabbath, that is the nations seeing the statutes kept. The other nations are expecting you to be that greedy individual that lacks integrity, a Judas who can be bought. We give them this right here: character and integrity, the hidden strength behind wisdom.

When Moses died, the mantle passed to Joshua, and the people answered him: “According as we hearkened unto Moses in all things, so will we hearken unto thee: only the Lord thy God be with thee, as he was with Moses.” They hearkened to Moses because they believed he was the man of the Lord. Moses led the people with integrity and character, even while judging Israel in the wilderness, and he kept that integrity all the way.

Yet there are negroes online, some elders from other camps, certain unsavory Black Hebrew Israelite camps, saying that Moses left the truth, that he was off and didn't have the spirit. What are you talking about? It says right there in verse 17: “only the Lord thy God be with thee, as he was with Moses.” The Lord was with Moses. Shame on you for not reading the scriptures, and shame on the men that follow you.

Because Sirach says, “Make not thyself an underling to a foolish man; neither accept the person of the mighty.” Camps like that have made themselves students and underlings to a negro that's just as dumb as they are.

Israel followed Joshua because they had seen Moses' character in him while he ministered under Moses. The company you keep matters. Joshua was under Moses, and Caleb did the same thing, and they learned integrity and good character by being under a man the Lord was with. Put yourself under a foolish man, and you learn his folly instead.

“But king Solomon loved many strange women, together with the daughter of Pharaoh”. When you turn against the Lord in this, you turn against your neighbor too, because you are taking foreign women. We know it will turn your heart away from following the Lord, but what does it do to your brother? It says you hate your brother. Tobit shows it.

“Beware of all whoredom, my son, and chiefly take a wife of the seed of thy fathers, and take not a strange woman to wife, which is not of thy father’s tribe”. He calls interracial marriage whoredom. “for we are the children of the prophets, Noe, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob: remember, my son, that our fathers from the beginning, even that they all married wives of their own kindred, and were blessed in their children, and their seed shall inherit the land.”

“Now therefore, my son, love thy brethren, and despise not in thy heart thy brethren, the sons and daughters of thy people, in not taking a wife of them”. Don’t despise your brethren. Passing over the daughters of your own people for strange women is despising your brethren in your heart. “for in pride is destruction and much trouble, and in lewdness is decay and great want: for lewdness is the mother of famine.”

That is exactly where Solomon went. The Lord had said of those nations, “Ye shall not go in to them, neither shall they come in unto you: for surely they will turn away your heart after their gods”, and Solomon clave unto them in love. His wives turned away his heart after Ashtoreth, Milcom, Chemosh and Molech, and he built high places for them and for all his strange wives. That is how syncretism enters: through the strange wife, and it begins by despising your own people.

Solomon offered “according to the commandment of Moses”, on the sabbaths, the new moons and the solemn feasts, “three times in the year”: the feast of unleavened bread, the feast of weeks and the feast of tabernacles. It is the same law given in Deuteronomy 16:16: “Three times in a year shall all thy males appear before the Lord thy God”, and “they shall not appear before the Lord empty.” So we are supposed to gather and give an offering three times a year. We come together.

But do we give a physical offering today? No. So what do we offer? We offer ourselves; we offer obedience. Sirach puts it plainly: “He that keepeth the law bringeth offerings enough: he that taketh heed to the commandment offereth a peace offering.”

Keeping the law is the offering. The one who takes heed to the commandment is not coming before the Lord empty; his obedience is his peace offering. That is how Israel keeps these feasts now, the feast of weeks, which is Pentecost, among them: by gathering together and bringing a life that keeps the commandments.

The nations have gods many and lords many, but a man who knows the one God, the Father, and the one Lord Jesus Christ can say, “we are ready to die, rather than to transgress the laws of our fathers.”

The third brother, when they came to cut him, put out his tongue right away and held forth his hands manfully: come on, let's get this over with. “Then I saw that she was defiled, that they took both one way, And that she increased her whoredoms: for when she saw men pourtrayed upon the wall, the images of the Chaldeans pourtrayed with vermilion, Girded with girdles upon their loins, exceeding in dyed attire upon their heads, all of them princes to look to, after the manner of the Babylonians of Chaldea”. Israel looked at the pictures of her enemies on the wall, dressed up like princes.

“And as soon as she saw them with her eyes, she doted upon them, and sent messengers unto them into Chaldea.” As soon as she saw them, she wanted them. That is why the Lord said in Numbers 15, when he gave us the fringes, that with your eyes you will go a whoring.

Ezekiel was shown “what the ancients of the house of Israel do in the dark, every man in the chambers of his imagery? for they say, The Lord seeth us not; the Lord hath forsaken the earth.” Seventy elders with censers in their hands, burning incense to the images in the dark.
