In the vessel were “all manner of fourfooted beasts of the earth, and wild beasts, and creeping things, and fowls of the air.” Peter had to explain to the circumcision, who contended with him, that the fourfooted beasts, the wild beasts, the creeping things and the fowls of the air refer to man. So there had to be scripture to prove it.

Ezra prays: “Let it not be thy will to destroy them which have lived like beasts; but to look upon them that have clearly taught thy law.” There are men who have lived like beasts, and Ezra pleads with God not to destroy them. So we know the beast refers to man.

The vision was not about animals; it was about men. Israel, scattered and living like beasts without the law, is what was let down in that sheet, and Ezra's prayer is that God would spare them and look upon those who teach his law.

The vessel also held “creeping things.” Who are the creeping things? The vision was not about animals; it was about man, so there has to be a scripture showing that the creeping thing refers to man. Habakkuk says to God: “And makest men as the fishes of the sea, as the creeping things, that have no ruler over them?”

Men made as creeping things that have no ruler over them. When we were without God, with no ruler, we were like creeping things, like insects or bugs. Without the laws of God, we were like beasts, like animals.

So every creature in Peter's sheet is a description of Israel scattered without God and without his law. The creeping things are men with no ruler over them, and God was about to bring them back under his rule.

The last creatures in the vessel are the “fowls of the air.” There had to be scripture to show that the fowls of the air also refer to man. Hosea says: “Ephraim also is like a silly dove without heart: they call to Egypt, they go to Assyria. When they shall go, I will spread my net upon them; I will bring them down as the fowls of the heaven; I will chastise them, as their congregation hath heard.”

Ephraim, the northern kingdom, is the silly dove, brought down as the fowls of the heaven. So the fowls in Peter's vision are Israelites too.

Now imagine those of the circumcision hearing Peter speak: listen, over here in Hosea, remember, God called us fowls. God was showing him it was time to gather the twelve tribes, north and south, back together.

That is why the scripture says prove all things. Everything must be proven as it is written, that thou mightest be justified in thy sayings, and overcome when thou art judged. Peter did not just tell a vision; he could prove every creature in it from the prophets.

Peter “saw heaven opened, and a certain vessel descending unto him, as it had been a great sheet knit at the four corners.” Now the scriptures substantiate the vision he had. What is the vessel? Hosea says: “Israel is swallowed up: now shall they be among the Gentiles as a vessel wherein is no pleasure.”

Israel was that vessel, a vessel among the Gentiles in which nobody had pleasure. Swallowed up among the nations, Israel was not wanted by anyone.

This is why the nations cannot handle us right now: when we speak, we can use the Bible to explain itself. When they hear Acts 10, they think it is everybody. No. God said Israel was the vessel. Peter's vision was not about the whole world coming in; it was about the scattered house of Israel, living among the Gentiles, being let down before him so that it could be gathered.

The vessel in Peter's vision was “knit at the four corners.” The four corners are in the prophets too: “And he shall set up an ensign for the nations, and shall assemble the outcasts of Israel, and gather together the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth.”

So what is in that sheet, gathered at the four corners? It was Israel, scattered through the four corners of the earth, living as beasts. The outcasts of Israel and the dispersed of Judah are the ones God assembles from those four corners.

He sets up an ensign “for the nations” because Israel would be scattered among all the nations and live as Gentiles. The picture of a sheet knit at four corners is the picture of God drawing his scattered people together from every end of the earth, and that is the vision Peter had to explain to those of the circumcision.

The vessel also held “wild beasts.” Isaiah names them: “Thy sons have fainted, they lie at the head of all the streets, as a wild bull in a net: they are full of the fury of the Lord, the rebuke of thy God.”

The sons of Israel, fainted and lying at the head of every street, are compared to a wild bull caught in a net, full of the fury of the Lord. The wild beast is a man of Israel under God's rebuke.

When Peter explained the fourfooted beasts and wild beasts, he would have to refer to scriptures like these. Remember, it is written in 2 Esdras that we lived as beasts. Remember, it is written in Psalms that we were as beasts. Remember, Isaiah the prophet said we would be as a wild bull. The vision was about men, and the scriptures prove it.

Another witness that the beasts in Peter's sheet are men: the psalmist says of himself, “So foolish was I, and ignorant: I was as a beast before thee.”

A man, foolish and ignorant before God, is called a beast. So when Peter explained the vision to those of the circumcision who contended with him, he could say: remember, it is written in Psalms that we were as beasts before God.

That is the whole key to Acts 10. The fourfooted beasts in the vessel are not pork and shellfish made clean. They are the people of Israel who were foolish and ignorant, living as beasts before the Lord, whom God was now going to cleanse and gather back together.

Baruch shows the word common used again for evil. Speaking of the idolaters and their gods, “they will give thereof to the common harlots, and deck them as men with garments, being gods of silver, and gods of gold, and wood.” The common harlots: the word goes with whoredom and idolatry.

So when Peter said, “I have never eaten any thing that is common or unclean”, he was saying, I have never dealt with sinners. I have never sat down with them.

But then the voice spake unto him again the second time, “What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common.” What had God cleansed? The subject matter is man. And to explain that cleansing to those of the circumcision, Peter would have to go to the Old Testament: to Ezekiel 37, where God would save them out of their dwelling places and cleanse them, take the children of Israel from among the heathen and make two kingdoms one; and to Hosea 1, where in the place where it was said unto them, Ye are not my people, it would be said, Ye are the sons of the living God.

The time had come to gather the northern kingdom back together. And that is happening now: God's people are being gathered in South America, in Africa and here in the States.

Peter answered the vision, “Not so, Lord; for I have never eaten any thing that is common or unclean.” To understand what he meant by common, go to Solomon: “There is an evil which I have seen under the sun, and it is common among men”.

Common is tied to evil. Peter understood that. So when he said he had never eaten anything common, he was not only talking about meat. In other words: I have never done sin, I have never dealt with sin, I have never dealt with people that were evil.

That is why the vision had to be explained to him. The sheet let down from heaven was not about food; it was about men, and Peter was being told to go among people he had counted as common.

On the day of Pentecost “suddenly there came a sound from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled all the house where they were sitting”, and “they were all filled with the Holy Ghost.” That Holy Ghost was the mighty wind that filled them.

Acts 4 shows the same thing again: “And when they had prayed, the place was shaken where they were assembled together; and they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and they spake the word of God with boldness.” The place shook, the Holy Ghost filled them, and the result was boldness.

When the apostles spoke and the Holy Ghost filled them, they were bold in what they said, because they knew what they were saying was sent of God, and they could prove it from the scriptures. That is the spirit that came on them at Pentecost: not a show, but a boldness to speak the word of God, grounded in knowing it.

The Holy Ghost came at Pentecost as a rushing mighty wind. Sirach tells of another man covered by the wind: “Elias it was, who was covered with a whirlwind: and Eliseus was filled with his spirit: whilst he lived, he was not moved with the presence of any prince, neither could any bring him into subjection.”

Look what it says next: “No word could overcome him; and after his death his body prophesied.” While the spirit of God was on him, no word could overcome him.

Men, study. When you are out in the street, there should be no word that can confound you. We should not be hearing men teaching who cannot explain basic scriptures. We are going up against, for the most part, Christians, and they don't know the Bible. We should know who we are and how to explain it: Galatians 3, Ephesians 2:11-16. This is very elementary.

When the spirit of God is on you, no word should be able to overcome you. That is what filled the apostles at Pentecost, and that is what should fill the men who go out to teach today.

At Pentecost the Holy Ghost came as a wind. Ezekiel was told to prophesy to the wind: “Prophesy unto the wind, prophesy, son of man, and say to the wind, Thus saith the Lord God; Come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe upon these slain, that they may live.” That is the word of God coming upon them.

“So I prophesied as he commanded me, and the breath came into them, and they lived, and stood up upon their feet, an exceeding great army.”

That is what was happening in Acts. They taught, and the people came in and gathered: devout men out of every nation under heaven, the scattered of Israel, hearing the word in their own tongues and standing up again.

All of you are here because the word of God was breathed on you, and it wasn't because the people teaching were shaky. So for you men out there teaching: study to shew thyself approved. The breath that raises the slain into an exceeding great army comes through a word that is taught with power.

At Pentecost they “began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance.” Other tongues means other languages. The psalm already said it: “There is no speech nor language, where their voice is not heard.”

There is no speech nor language where their voice is not heard. The devout men dwelling at Jerusalem came “out of every nation under heaven”, because according to Deuteronomy 28 we were going to be scattered into all nations. Every man heard the apostles speak in his own language, and they marvelled, “are not all these which speak Galileans?” That is because we were scattered among the heathen and learned their languages.

So God made sure the word reached every one of them in the tongue wherein they were born. In every language the scattered people of Israel had taken on, their voice was heard, and the gathering of the twelve tribes began.

When the voice told Peter, “What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common”, Peter would have had to go to the Old Testament to explain what God had cleansed. He would go to Ezekiel 37: “I will save them out of all their dwellingplaces, wherein they have sinned, and will cleanse them: so shall they be my people, and I will be their God.” And whom was he gathering, and from where? “Behold, I will take the children of Israel from among the heathen”: they were living among the Gentiles, the nations. He gathers them, cleanses them, and takes the two kingdoms, the stick of Judah and the stick of Joseph in the hand of Ephraim, and makes them one.

Hosea shows the same joining: “Then shall the children of Judah and the children of Israel be gathered together, and appoint themselves one head, and they shall come up out of the land: for great shall be the day of Jezreel.” That is the two sticks becoming one in the Lord's hand.

“Yet the number of the children of Israel shall be as the sand of the sea, which cannot be measured nor numbered; and it shall come to pass, that in the place where it was said unto them, Ye are not my people, there it shall be said unto them, Ye are the sons of the living God.” The northern kingdom, cast out among the heathen and called not my people, would be called the sons of the living God again. That was the prophecy, and that is why Peter could not call those men common: the time had come, Peter, we have to gather them together, bring them together.

And guess what: that is happening now. It has been going on since back then until now. We are out in South America gathering God's people, out in Africa gathering God's people, and here in the States bringing God's people back together, Judah and Israel under one head.

Christ said, “there shall be one fold, and one shepherd.” The fold he was speaking in was the Jews in Jerusalem, primarily Judah, Benjamin and Levi. The other sheep, not of that fold, were the rest of Israel, and he would gather the two nations, the southern and northern kingdoms, together under one shepherd, Jesus Christ.

Micah prophesied that one fold: “I will surely assemble, O Jacob, all of thee; I will surely gather the remnant of Israel; I will put them together as the sheep of Bozrah, as the flock in the midst of their fold: they shall make great noise by reason of the multitude of men.”

“all of thee” means all twelve tribes. That is the same thing Christ was saying: I have sheep that are not of this fold; them also I must bring, that there may be one fold and one shepherd. The prophecy was that all twelve tribes were going to be brought back together.

The beginning of it coming to fruition was when Christ came and began to teach, and his dying was the beginning of the twelve tribes being gathered back together. That is what his death was about: he was sent by his Father to gather the flock of Jacob into one fold.

Everything Christ and the apostles spoke was already spoken in what we call the Old Testament, and they used it to substantiate their points. So when Christ says of his other sheep, “they shall hear my voice”, the psalm already said it.

“O come, let us sing unto the Lord: let us make a joyful noise to the rock of our salvation.” The rock of our salvation is Christ. “For the Lord is a great God, and a great King above all gods. In his hand are the deep places of the earth”; “The sea is his, and he made it: and his hands formed the dry land. O come, let us worship and bow down: let us kneel before the Lord our maker.”

“For he is our God; and we are the people of his pasture, and the sheep of his hand. To day if ye will hear his voice.” We are the sheep of his hand, and the condition is the same: if you will hear his voice. That is exactly what Christ said in John 10: “them also I must bring, and they shall hear my voice.”

For all of us there was a time that we heard this voice. We heard the word of God, and it brought us to repentance, to change. Something innate in us made us acknowledge the word of God by hearing his voice and changing our life. That is how the sheep of his pasture are known.

The water Christ gives is “a well of water springing up into everlasting life”, and Paul shows what that understanding is. He is a minister of the gospel “which was preached to every creature which is under heaven”, to fulfil the word of God: “Even the mystery which hath been hid from ages and from generations, but now is made manifest to his saints”.

It was hid for ages that the northern kingdom had a part to play in this, to repent and come back. The ones who did understand were the learned men who studied, many of them the Pharisees, which is why they said, will he go to the dispersed among the Gentiles and teach them? They read Isaiah, Ezekiel and Deuteronomy. The masses didn't have the scriptures; the learned men had the parchment. But now he gave it to the apostles to teach.

“To whom God would make known what is the riches of the glory of this mystery among the Gentiles; which is Christ in you, the hope of glory”. The riches of this mystery among the Gentiles is that the northern kingdom has an opportunity of repentance: he is gathering back the Gentiles. The secret hid for ages is being revealed to the whole world; it is no longer gatekept. The apostles would go throughout the earth and teach the people that you are not Puerto Rican, you are not Dominican, whatever byword was given to you: you are the children of Israel. “Whom we preach, warning every man, and teaching every man in all wisdom”.

That is what is happening to us now. The understanding of this Bible and of who we are was hid for ages, but the Lord said in this hour the true worshippers are going to wake up.

Christ told her, “If thou knewest the gift of God, and who it is that saith to thee, Give me to drink; thou wouldest have asked of him, and he would have given thee living water.” What is the living water? A brother answered from Ephesians: “That he might sanctify and cleanse it with the washing of water by the word”.

You are cleansed by the washing of water by the word, so the living water is the word of God. What Christ would have given her was understanding: the understanding that the tribes were going to be gathered back together again.

She said, “Art thou greater than our father Jacob, which gave us the well”? That shows she understood she was part of the twelve tribes of Israel; she just knew the Jews had no dealings with them. And Christ answered, “Whosoever drinketh of this water shall thirst again: But whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst”. The water, the understanding he was going to give her, would bring about the kingdom and salvation for them, because they had been disconnected from it for so long.

Hosea shows why Ephraim was let alone. “Call her name Lo–ruhamah: for I will no more have mercy upon the house of Israel; but I will utterly take them away.” He would no longer have mercy on the house of Israel, because they fully went into idolatry. “But I will have mercy upon the house of Judah, and will save them by the Lord their God, and will not save them by bow, nor by sword, nor by battle, by horses, nor by horsemen”, as can be read in 2 Kings 19.

“Call his name Lo–ammi: for ye are not my people, and I will not be your God.” That was the message to the northern kingdom because of his anger at their idolatry: you will not be my people, and I will not be your God. That is why the woman said the Jews have no dealings with us.

But then it comes back: “Yet the number of the children of Israel shall be as the sand of the sea, which cannot be measured nor numbered; and it shall come to pass, that in the place where it was said unto them, Ye are not my people, there it shall be said unto them, Ye are the sons of the living God.” What is he saying? I am going to bring you back together again.

All the prophets spoke from a place of prophecy, judgment, and eventually redemption. That is what gives us hope to change and repent. If there were no endgame where we come out of this, there would be no incentive. But God said if you turn back to me, in the place where it was said you are not my people, there you will be called the sons of God.

The woman of Samaria said, “How is it that thou, being a Jew, askest drink of me, which am a woman of Samaria? for the Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans.” These Samaritans were Israelites who still lived there. Samaria is north of Jerusalem, as the map shows, and the Jews of Jerusalem stopped dealing with our people located in Samaria.

Why did that happen? A brother answered from Hosea: “Ephraim is joined to idols: let him alone.” That is why she said it. The scripture said Ephraim was joined to idols, and the word was to let him alone.

So the separation between the Jews and the Samaritans was not just a grudge; it grew out of the judgment on the northern kingdom for its idolatry. Judah took that word and left Ephraim alone. Yet here Christ, of Judah, sits at Jacob's well and asks a woman of Samaria to give him drink.

Before Hosea recorded the Lord casting off the house of Israel, Isaiah had already prophesied it: “For the head of Syria is Damascus, and the head of Damascus is Rezin; and within threescore and five years shall Ephraim be broken, that it be not a people.”

They already knew. God already told them that within sixty-five years Ephraim, the northern kingdom, would be broken and destroyed, and that is what Hosea 1 is recording: Lo–ruhamah, no more mercy on the house of Israel, and Lo–ammi, ye are not my people.

So when the woman of Samaria says the Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans, she is standing at the end of that prophecy. Ephraim was broken “that it be not a people”, cut off for idolatry. And that is exactly why it matters that Christ, a Jew, is speaking to her at Jacob's well: the people who were broken off are about to be offered the living water.

The woman at the well said, “Our fathers worshipped in this mountain”. On the map, the mountains above the well are Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal. Joshua 8 shows why she said it: “Then Joshua built an altar unto the Lord God of Israel in mount Ebal”, “an altar of whole stones, over which no man hath lift up any iron: and they offered thereon burnt offerings unto the Lord, and sacrificed peace offerings.” “And he wrote there upon the stones a copy of the law of Moses, which he wrote in the presence of the children of Israel.”

When we first came into the land, the first place we came into was what would be called Samaria, and the first altars were set up in Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim. That is why, when the nation split, the northern kingdom went back up top and worshipped there: this is the place where we worshipped initially. But God called his home Jerusalem; that is where he set up his temple.

Read on: “And all Israel, and their elders, and officers, and their judges, stood on this side the ark and on that side before the priests the Levites, which bare the ark of the covenant of the Lord, as well the stranger, as he that was born among them; half of them over against mount Gerizim, and half of them over against mount Ebal”. The blessings went up on the children of Israel, and the cursing was on Mount Ebal.

“There was not a word of all that Moses commanded, which Joshua read not before all the congregation of Israel, with the women, and the little ones, and the strangers that were conversant among them.” When we came into the land we had a mixed multitude of the other nations among us, and they were conversant in the laws of God. They had to learn the laws. We taught them how to keep the Sabbath day: six days you do your work, and on the seventh no work, neither your manservant, nor your maidservant, nor the stranger that is within thy gates.

Then Christ answered her: “Woman, believe me, the hour cometh, when ye shall neither in this mountain, nor yet at Jerusalem, worship the Father.” There was a time coming, 70 AD, when Jerusalem would be toppled by the Romans, and neither the mountains of Samaria nor Jerusalem would matter, because he was destroying it. His purpose was to gather in one the twelve tribes of Israel.

The New Testament shows the dispersed being taught: “And they are informed of thee, that thou teachest all the Jews which are among the Gentiles to forsake Moses, saying that they ought not to circumcise their children, neither to walk after the customs.” There were Jews among the Gentiles, and Paul was going to them.

We know from the text that the Jews were going to be dispersed among the Gentiles and live like Gentiles. Coming back to the New Testament, it shows Paul going out to find the Jews scattered among these other nations, living like Gentiles, living like strangers, living like heathens, and bringing them back to God.

This was the prophecy sent from the Old Testament: the job was to raise up the twelve tribes of Israel again. What the Jews in John 7 asked, “will he go unto the dispersed among the Gentiles”?, is exactly what was done.

Isaiah 11 says “he shall set up an ensign for the nations”. Why for the nations? Because Israel was going to be scattered: “And the Lord shall scatter thee among all people, from the one end of the earth even unto the other; and there thou shalt serve other gods, which neither thou nor thy fathers have known, even wood and stone.”

We were going to be scattered in all these nations and live as Gentiles, serving other gods. So the ensign set up for the nations is set up to “assemble the outcasts of Israel, and gather together the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth.” The ones he gathers out of the nations are Israel.

That is what the Jews meant in John 7 when they asked, “will he go unto the dispersed among the Gentiles”? They knew the curse: Israel scattered from one end of the earth to the other.

Ezekiel says the same: “And I scattered them among the heathen, and they were dispersed through the countries: according to their way and according to their doings I judged them.”

They're dispersed. Israel was scattered among the heathen and dispersed through the countries, judged according to their own ways and doings. The Pharisees and chief priests understood Ezekiel 36 and the dispersed, along with Isaiah 11 and Tobit 3. So when they asked, “Whither will he go, that we shall not find him? will he go unto the dispersed among the Gentiles, and teach the Gentiles?”, they were speaking of scattered Israel living among the heathen.

The Old Testament shows who was sent and why. “And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots”: that Branch is Christ, as Zechariah 6 shows. “And the spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of the Lord.”

Then: “and he shall not judge after the sight of his eyes, neither reprove after the hearing of his ears.” That is the same exact thing Christ said in John 5:30: “as I hear, I judge”, “I seek not mine own will, but the will of the Father which hath sent me.” The Branch out of Jesse does not judge by himself; he does the will of the one who sent him.

So what did God send him to do? Keep reading in the same chapter, and verse 12 tells it: to set up an ensign, assemble the outcasts of Israel and gather the dispersed of Judah. When Christ spoke in the New Testament, he was reiterating what the Old Testament already said, and the text substantiates it.

“And in that day there shall be a root of Jesse, which shall stand for an ensign of the people; to it shall the Gentiles seek: and his rest shall be glorious.” Who are the Gentiles here? The Jews in John 7 asked, “will he go unto the dispersed among the Gentiles, and teach the Gentiles?” The answer is Israel, and it is proven by staying in the passage.

“the Lord shall set his hand again the second time to recover the remnant of his people, which shall be left, from Assyria, and from Egypt, and from Pathros, and from Cush, and from Elam, and from Shinar, and from Hamath, and from the islands of the sea. And he shall set up an ensign for the nations, and shall assemble the outcasts of Israel, and gather together the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth.” The Gentiles that seek the root of Jesse are the outcasts of Israel, the remnant of his people.

That was God's will in sending his Son: to gather the twelve tribes of Israel. The Pharisees and chief priests were studied men. They understood this prophecy of the dispersed, which is why they asked whether he would go unto the dispersed among the Gentiles.

“Yet a little while am I with you, and then I go unto him that sent me.” Who sent Jesus? Christ answers it himself: “I can of mine own self do nothing: as I hear, I judge: and my judgment is just; because I seek not mine own will, but the will of the Father which hath sent me.”

He did not come on his own errand. He was sent from his Father, and he sought only the Father's will. And that will was to gather the twelve tribes of Israel: other sheep he must bring in, that there might be one fold and one shepherd. The gathering began when Christ came and began to teach, and his death was the beginning of the twelve tribes being brought back together.

So when he says he goes “unto him that sent me”, he is going back to the Father whose will he came to do. What that will was, the prophets had already written, and Isaiah 11 shows it.

“Ye shall seek me, and shall not find me: and where I am, thither ye cannot come.” The Old Testament already spoke it: “When your fear cometh as desolation, and your destruction cometh as a whirlwind; when distress and anguish cometh upon you. Then shall they call upon me, but I will not answer; they shall seek me early, but they shall not find me.”

They will not. The same words Christ spoke to the Pharisees and chief priests are written in Proverbs, against those who would not hear. When Christ, the apostles and the prophets spoke in the New Testament, their conversation was reiterating what the Old Testament was saying, and they could substantiate it with the text.

“And he will scourge us for our iniquities, and will have mercy again, and will gather us out of all nations, among whom he hath scattered us.” Again it uses the word nations, explaining that it was Israel being scattered among them.

The scourge is for our iniquities, but mercy comes again, and the promise is the gathering out of all nations. That is the same gathering Isaiah 11 speaks of, and the same work Christ was sent to begin: bringing the dispersed out from among the Gentiles, where they had been scattered.

Tobit shows the dispersed are Israel once again: “For they obeyed not thy commandments: wherefore thou hast delivered us for a spoil, and unto captivity, and unto death, and for a proverb of reproach to all the nations among whom we are dispersed.”

Israel disobeyed the commandments, and so was delivered for a spoil, into captivity, unto death, and made a proverb of reproach among all the nations where they were dispersed. The Pharisees understood Tobit and the dispersed, just as they understood Isaiah 11. That is why they said of Christ, “will he go unto the dispersed among the Gentiles, and teach the Gentiles?” They knew who the dispersed were.

Matthew writes “The land of Zabulon, and the land of Nephthalim, by the way of the sea, beyond Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles”, and Isaiah had already written it: “when at the first he lightly afflicted the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, and afterward did more grievously afflict her by the way of the sea, beyond Jordan, in Galilee of the nations.”

Matthew says “Galilee of the Gentiles”; Isaiah says “Galilee of the nations.” So the nations also means the Gentiles. Same land, same people, same word.

What we read in Matthew 4:15 was already recorded in the Old Testament. When the apostles and prophets spoke, they had to substantiate their points from what we call the Old Testament today. Whatever they said, they had to be able to justify it with that text. Matthew is not saying something new; he is showing the prophecy fulfilled.

This is the foundation for Acts 10. By the biblical text the Jews were going to be dispersed among the Gentiles and live like Gentiles, like strangers, like heathens. The New Testament shows Paul going out to find them scattered among the nations and bring them back to God, because the prophecy sent from the Old Testament was that the job was to raise up the 12 tribes of Israel again. The Gentiles of Galilee are Israelites that were scattered and cut off, and God is gathering them back.

That is how Daniel 7:25 is fulfilled: he thinks to change times and laws, and even the teaching of his religion is changed to keep our people from the laws and commandments of God.

“For thou art an holy people unto the Lord thy God”, chosen “above all people that are upon the face of the earth.” The nations know that. So they conspire to divide us and go out of their way to make sure we don't reproduce, because we are a problem to these nations: sterilizing our sisters with contraceptive shots, and doctors pressing a needle on an unborn child. Job 13:4 sums up what the Lord says concerning these physicians: “But ye are forgers of lies, ye are all physicians of no value.”

The Bible calls Esau, the white man, a forger of lies. Everything coming out of their mouths is lies. They are physicians of no value: not there to profit you, not there to give you the proper information so you can have a healthy family, an Israelite healthy family. They understand that the strength of the nation starts within the household, so they tell the sisters lies and they tell the husbands lies.

That is Deacon Malachi's experience. At a three-month checkup the doctors said they saw abnormalities and wanted to inject his unborn son to see if he was deformed; the needle could kill the baby, and if he was deformed there was nothing they could do. He was scared, and Satan whispered all kinds of things in his head, but he fasted and prayed, trusted in the Most High, and said to hell with these doctors. They saw his genes and knew who he was. Esau was trying to kill his son Benjamin, and Benjamin is standing in the class today. That is where faith comes in: trust in the Lord and leave everything to the Lord.

So seek counsel from the Lord and from the brothers and sisters set up as medical physicians, the licensed midwives and doulas of the school, before you go to these doctors, so you get a second opinion. What a doctor says is advice, not law. We are above all people in the eyes of God, and the physicians of the nations are not there for our good.

In Exodus 1 the new king says “the people of the children of Israel are more and mightier than we: Come on, let us deal wisely with them.” The Egyptians were tall and strong, yet they said the Hebrews were mightier; something had happened for them to know it. They could not destroy us head on, so they set up institutions of oppression to keep us beneath them. There is nothing new under the sun, and Jim Crow was already around in Joseph’s time.

Genesis 43:32: “And they set on for him by himself, and for them by themselves, and for the Egyptians, which did eat with him, by themselves: because the Egyptians might not eat bread with the Hebrews; for that is an abomination unto the Egyptians.”

Joseph had status. He was second over Egypt, the governor, the vizier, and still he was not granted the privileges of a full-blooded Egyptian. His Egyptian servants could not sit with him; they had their own table and he had his. He was a resource they could use, because his God gave him the dreams that kept them from famine, but he could not sit at their table because he was a Hebrew. It was an abomination for an Egyptian to eat with a Hebrew.

That is Jim Crow: Egyptians sit here, Hebrews sit there; whites sit here, coloreds sit there. The same people who used Joseph’s wisdom kept him apart, and the same thinking later dealt wisely with us in Egypt and in America.

Did it change after Joseph’s table? No. When his family came down, Joseph told them what to say to Pharaoh. “the men are shepherds, for their trade hath been to feed cattle;” and when Pharaoh asks, “What is your occupation?” they were to answer: “Thy servants’ trade hath been about cattle from our youth even until now, both we, and also our fathers: that ye may dwell in the land of Goshen; for every shepherd is an abomination unto the Egyptians.”

The Israelites were known as shepherds. Because of the war with the shepherd kings before Joseph arrived, the Egyptians hated shepherds, so the Israelites were despised twice over, as Hebrews and as shepherds.

So Israel was placed in Goshen, an isolated area away from the Egyptians. Egyptians and shepherds could not live in the same vicinity, which means there were no Egyptians living among us to put their blood into ours. That is segregation; that is redlining. It is nothing new.

That separation is the ground Exodus 1 grows out of. A people set apart, more and mightier than their masters, “dealt wisely” with: taskmasters over them, building Pithom and Raamses, serving “with rigour” in mortar, brick and “all manner of service in the field.” The same pattern followed us into America: set apart, built the Capitol and the White House, worked the fields.

The Lord called Bezaleel the son of Uri of the tribe of Judah and filled him “with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship”. A goldsmith, a silversmith, a brass worker, a stone cutter, a wood carver: one man. And with him Aholiab of the tribe of Dan, a partner.

Here is the work being done: “Then wrought Bezaleel and Aholiab, and every wise hearted man, in whom the Lord put wisdom and understanding to know how to work all manner of work for the service of the sanctuary, according to all that the Lord had commanded.”

Those two were the main men, and they had a team under them to create these things. “And Moses called Bezaleel and Aholiab, and every wise hearted man, in whose heart the Lord had put wisdom, even every one whose heart stirred him up to come unto the work to do it”.

We read of the tabernacle, the ark, the mercy seat, the furniture, the candlestick, the altars, the laver, the clothes of service, the holy garments tailored for Aaron, the anointing oil and the incense, and never realize who was behind making them. They did not fall out of the sky. Somebody made every one of them: our forefathers, filled with the wisdom of the Most High. Exodus 37:1-29 gives exactly what they made, in detail.

That is the superiority of the chosen people. The Bible means what it says: these were geniuses, and they were Israel.

“And Jacob was left alone; and there wrestled a man with him until the breaking of the day.” He fought for hours. In a real fight you are exhausted long before daybreak; a boxing match is twelve rounds, and Jacob fought until the break of day. “when he saw that he prevailed not against him, he touched the hollow of his thigh;” and put it out of joint. The angel had to dislocate Jacob’s thigh to stop him. Even then Jacob held on: “I will not let thee go, except thou bless me.”

“Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel: for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast prevailed.” That is what the name means: a prince with power with God.

Hosea 12:3-4 says why his name was changed: “He took his brother by the heel in the womb, and by his strength he had power with God: Yea, he had power over the angel, and prevailed: he wept, and made supplication unto him: he found him in Beth–el, and there he spake with us.” By his strength. His name was changed to Israel because of how strong he was. This was no slap boxing; it went back and forth, and there is no other record in the Bible of any man wrestling with an angel and prevailing. Jacob was a god on the earth.

He was trained to fight. Abraham had trained servants, armed them, and went to war to bring Lot back; Isaac knew it as well, and they taught Jacob. Imagine his descendants: David running through warriors, Samson, a warlike race. Our forefathers were intellectual as well as physically powerful; Abraham knew arithmetic and taught astronomy. That is why this superiority is stressed: white people, and even some of our own who move in their circles, say we are stupid and have low IQ, and many of us believe it. The white teacher told Malcolm X, top of his class, that being a lawyer was no profession for a nigga, and he should be a carpenter. The scriptures say otherwise about the children of Israel.

“Judah is a lion’s whelp.” He was a young lion in the 1960s, and after that he fell and became the old lion: “who shall rouse him up?” Then: “The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh come; and unto him shall the gathering of the people be.” Shiloh is Christ, and unto him, and to Judah, shall the gathering of the people be. Judah is the essential tribe to bring all twelve tribes together, the very liberation the 1969 hearings feared, which is why they said they had to destroy Judah among the African American community: education, revised Bibles, contraception, autism, using all they can to destroy these negroes.

Deuteronomy 33:7 is Moses’ blessing on the same tribe: “And this is the blessing of Judah: and he said, Hear, Lord, the voice of Judah, and bring him unto his people: let his hands be sufficient for him; and be thou an help to him from his enemies.” Bring Judah unto his people on an international scale: bring Judah to all the tribes, so that we can get out of here. Judah, Benjamin and Levi are giving these devils hell, and all twelve tribes are going to rise up together and bring hell to this kingdom.

It is already happening. A sister in Papua New Guinea wrote to one of our groups that her people thought they were free of colonization after independence in 1975, but religion still holds them colonized, enslaved, trapped and in poverty. Her answer was to go back to the origins of the Bible, obey it, and see what the Lord can do for their country: Genesis 49:8-12, and to listen to the tribe of Judah, who holds the sceptre, whom all tribes shall praise. Our people there know Judah has been sent to revive them.

That is why Judah in America is kept down. Every other tribe, in Jamaica, in Africa, in Europe, Levi speaking six languages, is better educated than Judah here. If Judah knew five or six languages, this thing would be over quickly. So the schools are dumbed down for Judah, while the blessing stands: the Lord will hear Judah’s voice, bring him to his people, and help him against his enemies.

Isaiah pronounces woe on them “that seek deep to hide their counsel from the Lord, and their works are in the dark, and they say, Who seeth us? and who knoweth us?” That is the council, meeting in the dark to make certain our people never rise up to who we are and never know who we are. The Most High turns their “turning of things upside down” right side up again, using his prophets.

Read on and see their end: “For the terrible one is brought to nought, and the scorner is consumed.” That is happening right now. The terrible one is the so-called white man today, and he is being brought to nothing; the scorners are consumed by destruction, by fire.

“and all that watch for iniquity are cut off”: all that search out iniquity shall be cut off, those “That make a man an offender for a word, and lay a snare for him that reproveth in the gate, and turn aside the just for a thing of nought.” The one that reproveth in the gate is us. The snares laid for the men who reprove them in the gate will not stand, because the Lord cuts off the ones who lay them.

After the terrible one is brought to nought, the Lord turns to Israel: “Therefore thus saith the Lord, who redeemed Abraham, concerning the house of Jacob, Jacob shall not now be ashamed, neither shall his face now wax pale.” The hidden counsel that kept us from knowing who we are will not keep us down any longer.

“But when he seeth his children, the work of mine hands, in the midst of him, they shall sanctify my name, and sanctify the Holy One of Jacob, and shall fear the God of Israel.” Our people are going to repent, turn to the Lord, and understand and acknowledge how superior we are according to the Lord.

“They also that erred in spirit shall come to understanding”: those who erred in spirit, who were in ignorance, in the world, carrying that inferiority complex, shall gain understanding. We shall come to learn who we are according to the Bible.

“and they that murmured shall learn doctrine”: those that spoke against the word of the Lord shall learn doctrine. This is the marvellous work and wonder of verse 14: the wisdom of the wise perishes, and the chosen people come to know themselves.

“Is Israel a servant? is he a homeborn slave? why is he spoiled?” The 1860 writer found us slaves everywhere: in Egypt when Karnak and Luxor were built, in Europe, Asia, Africa and America, at Thebes and Memphis, Babylon and Nineveh, Rome and Athens, Carthage and Constantinople, Havana and Richmond. He said slavery seems to be the history of this race and asked who will say slavery is not their doom. Were we meant to be in slavery all the time? Why are we conquered all the time? Because we keep breaking God's laws.

Read on to verse 21: “Yet I had planted thee a noble vine, wholly a right seed”. The Lord made us noble and made all of us righteous. We were superior; slavery was never our nature.

“how then art thou turned into the degenerate plant of a strange vine unto me?” We changed. Now we are a bunch of negroes: lost, destroyed, hating ourselves, hating our God, hating to do what he says, twerking everywhere and mumble rapping all this nonsense. We became a degenerate plant unto him.

So the answer to why Israel is spoiled is not that we were made to be slaves. The noble vine turned degenerate by breaking the laws of the God who planted it, and that is why we are spoiled among the nations.

The Lord pleads, “Withhold thy foot from being unshod, and thy throat from thirst”: turn to me, instead of lacking my commandments. “but thou saidst, There is no hope”. What did we say? Ain't no God.

“no; for I have loved strangers, and after them will I go.” We loved the nations, the heathens, and said we will go after them. There is no God; we are going to follow the white man, he is the hope, he is our god. That is why we are always in slavery.

I'mma follow the Persians: slavery. I'mma follow the Babylonians: slavery. The Greeks: slavery. The Romans: slavery. The Canaanites: slavery. Everywhere we go we follow the nations into slavery, all the time. Despite being superior to them, we want to follow them, and it does not make any sense. We are a rebellious people.

That is the answer to “Is Israel a servant? is he a homeborn slave? why is he spoiled?” We were not born slaves; we loved strangers and went after them, and every time they led us into captivity.

“Their visage is blacker than a coal”: their visage means their faces. It was already black; now it is blacker than a coal. “they are not known in the streets: their skin cleaveth to their bones; it is withered, it is become like a stick.” That is because of the famine, and Lamentations 5:10 says so: “Our skin was black like an oven because of the terrible famine.”

During a famine, when our people become malnourished or deprived of food and water, we become hypermelanated. Our skin gets darker because of the effects of famine. When white folks undergo famine, their lack of melanin heightens, and they become lighter than what they already are. So we got blacker because of the famine.

That also knocks down the doctrine that white people moved to a cold climate and that is how they became white. No, they were always that way. And the other side of it, that living on a black continent changed our complexion, is dumb, stupid science. Native Americans moved to Alaska and they are still brown. White people have been living over here since the 1700s; have any of them turned black? It is stupid doctrine.

So Lamentations proves the Israelites were already a black people, whose faces went blacker than a coal in the siege, not a white people darkened by the sun or turned pale by the cold.

“My son, keep the flower of thine age sound; and give not thy strength to strangers.” Your strength is your seed, your legacy. Do not give it to strangers. It is the same thing God said in Malachi: we dealt treacherously against the wife of our youth by giving our seed to Moab and Ammon and Edom.

“When thou hast gotten a fruitful possession through all the field, sow it with thine own seed, trusting in the goodness of thy stock.” The fruitful possession is a woman. The field is the world: our people are found all throughout the world. Sow that fruitful possession with your own seed, and trust in the goodness of your stock, because your woman is your stock; she is your kind. Her womb is the soil that belongs to you, the housing for gods, which is why God made one, “That he might seek a godly seed.”

“So thy race which thou leavest shall be magnified, having the confidence of their good descent.” Your race, your legacy, shall be magnified. The children know that daddy and mommy come from royalty: daddy is Judah, mama is Ephraim, the same nation of people. That child does not grow up confused and lost. Mix your seed with the nations and the child grows up confused, not knowing what it is, and shunned by both sides; it is like forcing a triangle peg into a square hole.

Marry your own and stick with your own people. Israel is a multi-featured, multicolored people, an assortment of beautiful colors and features, so there is no reason to step out of your nation. Wanting to step out means you despise yourself. Even the rich Edomite understands that the womb of our women carries genetic perfection, dominant superior genes.

“God standeth in the congregation of the mighty; he judgeth among the gods.” Who are the gods he judges among? The law answers it: “Thou shalt not revile the gods, nor curse the ruler of thy people.”

The gods and the ruler of thy people are the same men. The gods are our leaders, our judges. God always moved through the leadership of our forefathers: through Moses, through Aaron, through the captains and the officers. The spirit of the Lord would move and judge us through the leaders that were acting and moving correctly in that time.

So when the psalm says he judgeth among the gods, it is referring to our leaders, the men of Israel. That is why the psalm can go on to say “all the foundations of the earth are out of course”: when our leadership walked on in darkness and Israel went into sin, the world went out of order, because its rightful heirs and rulers are not in their proper place.

And that is why the Lord could say “Ye are gods; and all of you are children of the most High.” It was not a term of endearment; he meant it. The men of the children of Israel are gods, and because of that we cannot afford low self-esteem or an inferiority complex.

Ezekiel says, “And I will bring you into the wilderness of the people, and there will I plead with you face to face. Like as I pleaded with your fathers in the wilderness of the land of Egypt, so will I plead with you”. This is our deliverance from Babylon: we go back into the wilderness, Christ deals with us and teaches us the laws again, and what he is doing to us there is purging.

So what kind of pleading is he going to be doing? Is it baby, baby, please? No. The pleading is killing and smiting, and Isaiah proves it: “For, behold, the Lord will come with fire, and with his chariots like a whirlwind, to render his anger with fury, and his rebuke with flames of fire. For by fire and by his sword will the Lord plead with all flesh”. It's not a damn R&B song.

That is the same fury Ezekiel speaks of: “surely with a mighty hand, and with a stretched out arm, and with fury poured out, will I rule over you”. As he pleaded with our fathers in the wilderness of Egypt, where the rebellious fell, he will plead with us, by fire and by the sword.

So even after the deliverance there is still going to be a purge. There will still be bad actors among us, people that still need to get right, and they are going to get it; Christ is the one who will give it to them.

The Lord pleads with the nations the same way he pleads with Israel. Joel says: “I will also gather all nations, and will bring them down into the valley of Jehoshaphat, and will plead with them there for my people and for my heritage Israel”. No baby, baby, please for them either. He will kill them, for his people Israel.

The nations are judged “for my people and for my heritage Israel, whom they have scattered among the nations, and parted my land.” The pleading in the valley of Jehoshaphat is the Lord's vengeance on the ones who scattered us.

So when Ezekiel says the Lord will plead with Israel face to face in the wilderness “Like as I pleaded with your fathers in the wilderness of the land of Egypt”, the word means the same thing it means for the nations: judgment, smiting and fire, not begging. He pleads for Israel against the nations, and he pleads with the rebels in Israel in the wilderness, and nobody should read either as the Lord asking nicely.

Ezekiel says, “And I will purge out from among you the rebels, and them that transgress against me”. What kind of purge is he going to be doing? Killing. Matthew shows it: “Whose fan is in his hand, and he will throughly purge his floor, and gather his wheat into the garner; but he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire.” Does anybody not understand that?

The wheat is gathered into the garner, and the chaff is burned. That is the rebels who “shall not enter into the land of Israel”. Zechariah is still talking about the purge: “in all the land, saith the Lord, two parts therein shall be cut off and die; but the third shall be left therein.” And even the third that is left still has to be sifted, refined, made right, purged.

The Lord is not going to give the kingdom to wicked negroes. The kingdom will not be open to wicked negroes. To get the kingdom you have to go through this fire and get right; there is no other way. You can't keep doing what you do and think you are going to get the kingdom. It is impossible.

That is why we have to fight for this and help each other. If I see you weak and say nothing to you, that means I hate you. So if I tell you, bro, you have to fix that, and you say I hate you, shut your ass up; I am trying to save your life. We are so used to not taking correction from each other that it feels like hate, because everybody has coddled you, and you keep kicking the can down the street until you are back on the corner doing what you do. The fan is already in his hand.

Zechariah says, “I will bring the third part through the fire, and will refine them as silver is refined, and will try them as gold is tried”. In that fire some want to quit, stop relying on the brotherhood and abandon ship. Sirach shows why: “In the day of prosperity there is a forgetfulness of affliction: and in the day of affliction there is no more remembrance of prosperity.”

In the day when things are going well, you forget what it was like to be in your lowest state, and you have to take heed lest you fall. And in the day of affliction, when the fire comes up and the heat gets turned up, you forget the prosperity: the last end, the increase the Lord is going to give you, the things he has in store.

The trying of your faith worketh patience, and Sirach 2 says, woe unto them that have lost patience. If you would just purge your spirit, you would be able to receive all the things the Lord has promised for the future. But you quit because you forgot what the goal was; you forgot the mission, so you want to abandon ship.

When you are going through that adversity, be patient in your lowest state and don't forget the prosperity to come. That is what strengthens your faith through the refining, until the Lord says, “It is my people: and they shall say, The Lord is my God.”

Zechariah says two parts shall be cut off and die and the third brought through the fire. We are still talking about the purge. Christ describes what the purge looks like among the people: “And then shall many be offended, and shall betray one another, and shall hate one another.”

In this purging process a lot of people are going to turn their back to the Lord. That is what people forget: you are not turning your back to us. We are nothing but humble servants of the Lord, working together in the vineyard. You are turning your back to the Master and saying, I don't want to do the work anymore. And when you turn your back to your brother, it is called betrayal.

“And many false prophets shall rise, and shall deceive many.” That is the one who says, I can do the work outside the body; I don't have to be here; I can do my own thing. If you were going to do the work somewhere else, why wouldn't you do it here and continue the mission? Because you were never going to do the work; you had no intentions of doing it. And they deceive the simple. A brand new fool with the Bishop's precept book starts his own thing, while leadership has laboured twenty-plus years to do this work, and other fools follow him.

“And because iniquity shall abound, the love of many shall wax cold.” Iniquity, the short word is sin. “But he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved.” Fight until the end: that is the only way you get salvation. You have to walk through hell to get to heaven. There is no shortcut and no roundabout to the kingdom; you walk straight through. If you don't want to do it, don't do it.

When Joseph’s brothers sat down to eat bread, they saw “a company of Ishmeelites came from Gilead with their camels bearing spicery and balm and myrrh, going to carry it down to Egypt.” Judah said, “What profit is it if we slay our brother, and conceal his blood? Come, and let us sell him to the Ishmeelites.” Then the verse changes names: “Then there passed by Midianites merchantmen; and they drew and lifted up Joseph out of the pit, and sold Joseph to the Ishmeelites for twenty pieces of silver.”

There are always questions about the Midianites and the Ishmaelites. Genesis 25 shows who the Midianites were: “Then again Abraham took a wife, and her name was Keturah. And she bare him Zimran, and Jokshan, and Medan, and Midian, and Ishbak, and Shuah.” Keturah had six sons by Abraham, and Midian is one of them. The chapter goes on to his sons: “And the sons of Midian; Ephah, and Epher, and Hanoch, and Abida, and Eldaah. All these were the children of Keturah.”

So the Midianites are Abraham’s children through Keturah, just as the Ishmaelites are Abraham’s children through Hagar. They were working together and roaming the land together, all Abraham’s kids, and they looked very similar. That is why the story says Ishmaelites, then Midianites, then “the Midianites sold him into Egypt unto Potiphar,” and then in Genesis 39 Potiphar “bought him of the hands of the Ishmeelites.” It is not a contradiction; these groups were together.

Genesis 37 names both groups in the sale of Joseph: the Midianites drew him out of the pit and “sold Joseph to the Ishmeelites for twenty pieces of silver,” and later “the Midianites sold him into Egypt unto Potiphar.” Genesis 25:12 shows who the Ishmaelites were: “Now these are the generations of Ishmael, Abraham’s son, whom Hagar the Egyptian, Sarah’s handmaid, bare unto Abraham.”

Abraham had Ishmael from Hagar, and Ishmael had sons as well: Nebajoth the firstborn, “and Kedar, and Adbeel, and Mibsam, And Mishma, and Dumah, and Massa, Hadar, and Tema, Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah.” “These are the sons of Ishmael, and these are their names, by their towns, and by their castles; twelve princes according to their nations.”

Abraham’s children from Keturah and Abraham’s children from Hagar always lived together and worked together. So when a company of Ishmaelites comes by carrying spices down to Egypt and Midianite merchantmen are among them, it is one caravan of Abraham’s other children traveling side by side.

Meanwhile the brothers, so envious of Joseph, dipped his coat of many colours in the blood of a kid of the goats and let Jacob believe “an evil beast hath devoured him.” Reuben had suggested the pit so he could come back and save him, and when he returned, “Joseph was not in the pit; and he rent his clothes.” Envy will have you do evil things. Remember Reuben’s character; it plays a part later.

Joseph was seventeen, a teenager, sold into Egypt: “Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh, captain of the guard, an Egyptian, bought him of the hands of the Ishmeelites.” Yet “the Lord was with Joseph, and he was a prosperous man.” His master “saw that the Lord was with him, and that the Lord made all that he did to prosper in his hand,” and made him overseer over his house, putting all that he had into his hand.

Luke 16:10 explains why: “He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much: and he that is unjust in the least is unjust also in much.” Joseph was in slavery, but he was faithful to Potiphar, and Potiphar raised him up.

It speaks to us today. Many brothers and sisters have jobs, and the Most High is observing us in whatever we do. The least that we are faithful in is these little jobs out here. Just as Joseph was in captivity, we are in captivity, but that does not mean we can steal, lie or rob. When you are on your jobs, do not steal; deal right. God is watching each and every one of us.

And look what faithfulness brought: “the Lord blessed the Egyptian’s house for Joseph’s sake; and the blessing of the Lord was upon all that he had in the house, and in the field.” The theme is the same as when Jacob worked for Laban all those years and Laban was blessed for Jacob’s sake. Faithful in little, Joseph was trusted with much, until his master “knew not ought he had, save the bread which he did eat.”

When Potiphar’s wife could not get her way, she lied. She called the men of her house and said, “See, he hath brought in an Hebrew unto us to mock us; he came in unto me to lie with me, and I cried with a loud voice.” Then “she laid up his garment by her, until his lord came home”: she kept his clothes as false evidence, and told her husband the same lie.

Sirach shows what that kind of tongue does: “A backbiting tongue hath disquieted many, and driven them from nation to nation: strong cities hath it pulled down, and overthrown the houses of great men.” Somebody that lies on you can do much destruction. Joseph was the greatest man in Potiphar's house, trusted with everything, and a lying tongue brought him down to the king's prison.

It is the same today. Many brothers have been locked up because a woman lied on them: an ex-wife or ex-girlfriend who wants his life to go down the tubes, who calls him over, is refused, and then threatens to tell the police he hurt her. Others are in jail because a woman started a fight and expected him to defend her. Don't deal with a woman like that; that is the kind of woman Joseph had over him.

And this same spirit met our people in slavery. A lot of us were put to death because of it. Emmett Till was put to death for the lying woman, and there are a lot of cases like that. What Potiphar's wife did to Joseph, a backbiting tongue has done to Israel again and again.

Sirach goes on: “Many have fallen by the edge of the sword: but not so many as have fallen by the tongue.” The tongue does a lot of evil, and that is exactly what Potiphar’s wife did to Joseph. She never lifted a sword against him; she only spoke, and her words did the work.

She told her husband, “The Hebrew servant, which thou hast brought unto us, came in unto me to mock me,” and “when his master heard the words of his wife,” “his wrath was kindled.” On nothing but her word, “Joseph’s master took him, and put him into the prison, a place where the king’s prisoners were bound.” Remember how old Joseph is here: 17.

That is how our people have fallen too: brothers in prison on a lie, and in slavery times men like Emmett Till put to death because of a lying woman's words. More have fallen by the tongue than by the sword. Guard yourself from the kind of company that can destroy you with a word.

Joseph was 17, falsely accused, and thrown into the king's prison. Sirach tells you why this should not shock a servant of God: “My son, if thou come to serve the Lord, prepare thy soul for temptation.” Joseph understood this, because his father Jacob taught him.

“Set thy heart aright, and constantly endure, and make not haste in time of trouble.” Make not haste means don't leave this truth in your time of trouble. Satan will tell you, if you weren't in that Bible you wouldn't be going through half of what you're going through; you had it better when you served me. “Cleave unto him, and depart not away, that thou mayest be increased at thy last end.”

“Whatsoever is brought upon thee take cheerfully, and be patient when thou art changed to a low estate.” Joseph's family was rich; Jacob was a wealthy man. Joseph was taken from all that, sold as a slave, and now he is in the midst of poverty, in prison, for a crime he refused to commit. That is a low estate, and he bore it without leaving God.

Just as it goes for us, it went for our father Joseph. Israel today has been brought down to a low estate, and the tests and trials come because we serve the Lord. Endure them, cleave unto him, and you will be increased at your last end, as Joseph was.

Even in prison, “the Lord was with Joseph, and shewed him mercy, and gave him favour in the sight of the keeper of the prison.” The keeper “committed to Joseph’s hand all the prisoners that were in the prison,” and “looked not to any thing that was under his hand; because the Lord was with him, and that which he did, the Lord made it to prosper.”

Solomon gives the reason: “When a man’s ways please the Lord, he maketh even his enemies to be at peace with him.” That is what happened with Joseph. He was a Hebrew slave, accused of attacking his master's wife, locked in the place where the king's prisoners were bound, and his very jailer became favourable to him and handed him the whole prison.

It is the same pattern all through Joseph's life: in Potiphar's house the Lord blessed the Egyptian's house “for Joseph’s sake,” just as Laban was blessed for Jacob's sake when Jacob worked for him. Joseph's ways pleased the Lord; he refused sin even when it cost him, and whatever he did, the Lord made it to prosper. Keep your ways pleasing to God, and he will make even those set over you in captivity to be at peace with you.

Potiphar’s wife cast her eyes upon Joseph and said, “Lie with me.” Joseph refused, and he did not refuse half-heartedly: “how then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?” Notice he was not blaming God that he was a slave in a strange land. His master had kept nothing back from him “but thee, because thou art his wife,” and Joseph would not touch her.

This was not a single moment. “she spake to Joseph day by day”; she was trying to wear him down day by day. And the Egyptians loved beautiful women; remember when Abraham went down into Egypt, Sarah was in danger because of her beauty. Potiphar’s wife was no ugly woman; she was good on the eyes, and Joseph, at 17 years old, still said no. When she finally “caught him by his garment,” “he left his garment in her hand, and fled, and got him out.”

Sirach gives the precept for what Joseph did: “Flee from sin as from the face of a serpent: for if thou comest too near it, it will bite thee: the teeth thereof are as the teeth of a lion, slaying the souls of men.” Joseph saw sin like a snake, and he ran like a rabbit. If a snake fell into the room right now, everybody would be out of there. That snake is your sin. “All iniquity is as a two edged sword, the wounds whereof cannot be healed.”

Everybody's demon is not the same. For some it is food; for most of the brothers it is sexual demons, and those demons will get you. The butler and the baker of the king of Egypt offended their lord and were put in ward “the place where Joseph was bound.” “they dreamed a dream both of them, each man his dream in one night,” and in the morning they were sad, because “there is no interpreter of it.” Joseph answered, “Do not interpretations belong to God? tell me them, I pray you.”

Sirach speaks to dreams: “The hopes of a man void of understanding are vain and false: and dreams lift up fools.” “Whoso regardeth dreams is like him that catcheth at a shadow, and followeth after the wind.” Don't chase dreams; a man who lives by every dream is grasping at shadows.

But verse 3 gives a clue to understanding the dreams that come from God: “The vision of dreams is the resemblance of one thing to another, even as the likeness of a face to a face.” You may dream about somebody you know, say a man named Joe, and see Joe's face; but it is not Joe. It is someone similar to Joe, maybe in age or in what they do for a living. It could be Bob. You just have to know the people in your circle.

That is how the dreams in Genesis 40 work. The butler's vine with “three branches” and the baker's “three white baskets” were resemblances of one thing to another: the three branches and the three baskets were three days. The interpretation belonged to God, and Joseph gave it.

Jeremiah says the same thing Job said: “Cursed be the day wherein I was born: let not the day wherein my mother bare me be blessed.” Two prophets, and neither one blessed the day of his birth. Put that together with Pharaoh's birthday in Genesis 40, where the baker was hanged at the feast.

We never celebrated birthdays. They are days of narcissism, days to put ourselves up above God. The custom came from the nations; it came through the white man, who got it from what they dug up in their archaeological digs, and then taught that we should be celebrating birthdays.

Joseph's interpretations came to pass “the third day, which was Pharaoh’s birthday, that he made a feast unto all his servants.” On that birthday “he restored the chief butler unto his butlership again,” “But he hanged the chief baker: as Joseph had interpreted to them.”

Wherever you read of a birthday in scripture, Pharaoh's birthday, Herod's birthday, the birthday of one of the Greek kings, something bad happens. Here a man is hanged at a birthday feast. A birthday is a day of narcissism, a day of proclaiming yourself to be God.

Job shows how the Hebrews felt about the day of their birth: “Let the day perish wherein I was born, and the night in which it was said, There is a man child conceived.” A righteous man did not exalt the day he was born; he wished it would perish. That is why we never celebrated birthdays.

After interpreting the butler's dream, Joseph asked him, “think on me when it shall be well with thee,” and “make mention of me unto Pharaoh, and bring me out of this house:” “For indeed I was stolen away out of the land of the Hebrews: and here also have I done nothing that they should put me into the dungeon.” He wanted out of that dungeon.

Notice the prison is called a dungeon. Lamentations uses the same word: “They have cut off my life in the dungeon, and cast a stone upon me.” To cast a stone upon him means he would never get out. It is speaking of Israel in captivity.

That goes with our political prisoners, who have been in there for a long time, cut off in the dungeon with a stone cast over them. Joseph, stolen away and imprisoned though he had done nothing, is a picture of his people in captivity.

“at the end of two full years” Pharaoh dreamed of seven fat kine eaten up by seven lean kine, and seven good ears devoured by seven thin ears “blasted with the east wind.” None of the magicians could interpret it, until the chief butler remembered his faults and told Pharaoh of the young Hebrew. “Then Pharaoh sent and called Joseph, and they brought him hastily out of the dungeon: and he shaved himself, and changed his raiment, and came in unto Pharaoh.”

Solomon wrote the precept: “Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings; he shall not stand before mean men.” The business is God's business. Joseph was diligent in it in Potiphar's house and in the prison, and now a slave out of the dungeon stands before the king of Egypt. Even there he gave God the glory: “It is not in me: God shall give Pharaoh an answer of peace.”

And he did not come to Pharaoh with only a problem. To every problem, brothers, we must have a solution. Some spirits among us have a problem for every solution; stay away from brothers and sisters like that.

So Pharaoh said, “Can we find such a one as this is, a man in whom the Spirit of God is?” He put his ring upon Joseph's hand, arrayed him in fine linen, made him ride in the second chariot, “and they cried before him, Bow the knee.” We are going to tell the nations that too: bow the knee. “Joseph was thirty years old when he stood before Pharaoh”; he went in at 17 and spent 13 years in servitude and prison before he stood before the king.
